paper_title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Computer-use agents (CUAs) extend the capabilities of large language models from generating responses to operating computers and automating software tasks (Zhang et al., 2025b, Wang et al., 2025b). They can invoke software functions through application programming interfaces (APIs) and command-line interfaces (CLIs). Graphical user interfaces (GUIs) extend this access to functions that applications do not expose programmatically, providing critical last mile for software automation (Zhang et al., 2025a,c). Through GUI interaction, agents interpret the screen and translate natural-language goals into mouse and keyboard actions. Advances in visual grounding and action generation have expanded the range of operations these agents can perform (Qin et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025c, Zhou et al., 2025). As agents combine these operations into longer workflows, earlier actions shape the software state on which later decisions depend. Reliable completion requires agents to preserve intermediate progress and the users constraints, adapt to changing interfaces, and recover from errors while keeping the overall goal in view (Zhang et al., 2026, Lu et al., 2026). Training agents to coordinate such workflows therefore requires experience that develops precise interface skills and connects successive decisions to complete task outcomes. Obtaining this experience at scale begins with constructing varied tasks, each of which needs request grounded in available software and content, usable initial environment, and reliable way to judge success (Ge et al., 2026, Zhou et al., 2026b). Once these tasks are available, collecting experience from them requires an agent framework that sustains long interactions and records decisions and outcomes across desktop and web environments. The resulting demonstrations can teach the policy how to complete workflows, but independent execution may lead it into states absent from those demonstrations. Continued improvement therefore requires fresh interaction and outcome feedback from the policys own attempts (Wang et al., 2025c, Jung et al., 2026, Lu et al., 2026). Meeting these linked needs calls for co-designing how tasks are constructed, how agents execute them, and how the resulting experience is used for learning. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Our central idea is to co-design the production and use of experience, making software interaction continuing source of learning. We connect executable tasks to policy updates through three components (Figure 2), focusing on GUI-based software operation. The Experience Flywheel constructs executable tasks for the NorthCUA Harness to run and assess. The recorded trajectories and outcome evidence guide curation, supplying Staged Learning with demonstrations that complement the Flywheels separately constructed grounding examples. This mixture develops interface understanding and workflow completion. Shared execution and outcome interfaces also let the learner collect fresh attempts from the policy itself, extending the same system from demonstration collection to continued policy improvement. full-lifecycle infrastructure. We design the NorthCUA Harness as fullNorthCUA Harness: lifecycle infrastructure that executes software tasks and turns the resulting attempts into inspectable experience for learning. This requires keeping the agents decisions connected to its workspace and outcomes, from environment preparation through execution and evaluation to record preservation. Within the shared runtime, visual context and task memory help agents build on progress across long workflows (Zhang et al., 2026, 2025d). An evaluator uses the execution record and live workspace to check task completion and execution quality, supplementing task-specific verifiers where their coverage is incomplete (Zhuge et al., NorthCUA Technical Report 2 / NorthCUA 1 Introduction Figure 2. To scale this process, the Batch Rollout Service coordinates parallel workers and overlaps lifecycle stages, supporting eﬀicient, high-concurrency experience collection (Section 3). Experience Flywheel: scaling grounding and agentic experience. With runtime for collecting and checking software experience, the next challenge is to supply enough varied, useful work for the agent to learn. The Experience Flywheel addresses two levels of supervision: single-step grounding examples for locating controls and assessed agent trajectories for completing tasks. Grounding pairs screenshots with queries and target locations. Visual and structural annotations provide broad coverage (Lu et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025a), while application documentation NorthCUA Technical Report 3 / 123 NorthCUA 1 Introduction helps explain controls function when appearance alone is insuﬀicient. At the trajectory level, three complementary construction routes supply tasks to the harness. Scaling Intents derives requests from available software and content, while Scaling Environments builds the workspaces needed by sourced requests or reconstructs reference websites. For tasks with executable checks, Scaling Verifiers creates further tasks by adapting requests, initial states, and verifiers together (Ge et al., 2026, Lu et al., 2026, Lv et al., 2026). When valid task remains unsolved in ordinary collection, we use recursive self-improvement (RSI) for hard-task collection. Skill-guided exploration retains tested procedures for later attempts, while milestone-guided search preserves software states and agent context at verified milestones to explore alternative ways of completing the remaining work. Task outcomes and execution quality determine which trajectories become demonstrations for learning (Section 4). Staged Learning: from experience to capability. models ability to coordinate long workflow builds on familiarity with the interfaces and operations it uses. Staged Learning follows this progression, starting with Broad GUI mid-training on grounding examples and desktop and web trajectories judged to complete their tasks (Wang et al., 2025c, Jung et al., 2026). The broad trajectory corpus spans over four million GUI interaction steps across dozens of applications. Building on this operational foundation, Verified long-horizon supervised fine-tuning (SFT) concentrates on carefully selected, complete workflows whose outcomes pass executable task verifiers and whose intermediate results support later decisions. Independent execution can still lead the policy into states absent from its demonstrations. Joint desktopweb agentic reinforcement learning therefore lets one policy practice in both domains and learn from fresh successes and failures. Task verifiers score these attempts, and group-relative policy optimization (GRPO, Shao et al., 2024) uses their outcomes to update the policy (Section 5). Shared task, execution, and assessment interfaces connect these learning stages to experience collection (Figure 2). An updated policy can return to the same Harness, where its new attempts are evaluated and can be curated into subsequent training experience. This return path lets advances in model capability support further collection, giving NorthCUA reusable foundation for continued learning across desktop and web environments. The resulting NorthCUA family comprises Nano (9B), Mini (35B), and Pro (397B), all built on Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026a). We evaluate this family on six benchmarks spanning GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction. The suite follows the agent from locating controls to completing long workflows and checking whether Web applications behave as intended. NorthCUA establishes state-of-the-art results among open-source models in all three domains (Figure 1). With 397B parameters, Pro outperforms trillion-parameter Qwen3.8Max and Kimi-K3 on both grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified (Qwen Team, 2026c, Kimi Team, 2026). The 35B Mini also surpasses Kimi-K3 on OSWorldVerified and Qwen3.8-Max on WebArena-Verified. Stage comparisons show desktop and Web gains across all three model sizes after long-horizon SFT and joint RL (Section 6). Long workflows also accumulate the latency of successive model decisions. To reduce this cost, NorthCUA-Ultrafast adapts pre-RL Nano with Jev-inspired choice head, selecting finite actions directly while retaining generation for open-ended outputs (Almeida, 2026). Its Head + LoRA variant completes matched successful WebArena-Verified tasks 2.3 faster on average than full generation (Section 6.8). We release all three models, the full NorthCUA Harness code, and this technical report, providing an open foundation for developing agents that carry software work from user intent to completed outcomes. sections.title: 2.1 Task Scope and Characteristics
sections.content: We study two capability targets in desktop and web environments (Figure 3): locating requested control in screenshot and completing task through software interaction. We evaluate these targets separately. Single-step UI grounding. Given screenshot and natural-language query, the model predicts the coordinates (x, y) of the target UI element in the original image (Cheng et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025b). The model completes the task with one prediction over fixed screenshot. The query can describe the elements appearance or function, such as locating the zoom tool in Figure 3(a). Figure 3. Task scope and interaction. (a) Single-step grounding predicts target location in fixed screenshot. The enlarged output view marks the zoom tool, with absolute pixel coordinates in the original image. (b) Desktop and web agents change software state through successive actions, with completion assessed from the resulting artifacts or state. Web observations also include DOM information. Generated GUI scenes, action overlays, and outcomes are illustrative. The displayed transitions omit intermediate interactions. NorthCUA Technical Report 5 / NorthCUA 2.2 System Organization and Experience Lifecycle End-to-end computer use. An end-to-end task combines user request, an initial software environment, and conditions for judging completion. The environment provides the applications, files, and website records needed for the request. The agent observes the current state, takes an action, and uses the resulting feedback to decide what to do next. Later decisions can use information and results from earlier steps. The request and completion conditions stay fixed throughout the attempt, so the final files or software state can be checked against the original goal (Zhou et al., 2024, Xie et al., 2024). Figure 3(b) illustrates the two interaction settings: Desktop agents observe desktop screenshots and operate applications through mouse and keyboard actions, including clicking, typing, scrolling, and dragging. Tasks may span multiple applications and files. Web agents observe webpage screenshots and document object model (DOM) information, and interact through browser tools for navigation, element-based or coordinate-based actions, text input, and tab management. Both settings follow the same observation, action, and feedback loop, using their respective desktop or browser interfaces. The acting policy uses these interfaces to perform the task. Preparation, annotation, and evaluation can use additional programmatic tools with separate permissions.

sections.title: 2.2 System Organization and Experience Lifecycle
sections.content: The experience loop in Figure 2 connects task construction to execution and learning. Its handoffs specify how an executable task becomes an assessed record and then training sample. The Experience Flywheel packages each executable task as CaseSpec, task specification containing the request, input materials, environment configuration, and setup instructions, together with requirements for assessing the result. For the invoice task in Figure 3(b), this means providing the workbook and spreadsheet application and specifying that the exported PDF should highlight overdue invoices. Using this specification, the NorthCUA Harness prepares the environment, uploads input files, and runs setup and launch commands before starting the agent on the request. Observations, actions, and feedback are recorded throughout the attempt so that its outcome can be assessed in the context of the work that produced it. Task-specific checks, an evaluator, or both inspect the result against the declared requirements. For the invoice task, this means checking the saved PDF and its highlighted contents. These outcome and execution-quality assessments give the Experience Flywheel the evidence needed to select demonstrations. Valid tasks that remain unsolved can instead enter the hard-task collection branch, where skill-guided exploration or milestoneguided search produces further attempts for the same assessment process (Section 4.3). Staged Learning turns this collected experience into capability in three steps. Broad GUI midtraining combines diverse task trajectories with the Flywheels separate screenshotquerytarget examples, building foundation in interface understanding and software operation. Grounding supervision is used only in this stage. Verified long-horizon SFT then focuses on high-quality, complete workflows with checked outcomes, teaching the policy to carry information and intermediate results across dependent steps. This prepares the model to learn further from its own interaction. For joint desktopweb agentic reinforcement learning, we first select tasks on which the SFT policys trial attempts have different outcomes. This focuses initial collection on tasks with useful NorthCUA Technical Report 6 / 123 NorthCUA 3 NorthCUA Harness: Full-Lifecycle Infrastructure for Computer Use outcome differences for comparing executions. The Harness collects fresh groups of attempts, executable verifiers score their outcomes, and GRPO uses comparisons within each task group to update one shared policy (Section 5.3). The updated policy returns to the Harness for subsequent attempts under the same task and outcome interfaces. The following sections explain these components in detail. Section 3 presents the execution and assessment framework, Section 4 describes task construction and experience curation, and Section 5 develops the staged learning recipe.

sections.title: 3 NorthCUA Harness: Full-Lifecycle Infrastructure for Computer Use
sections.content: The NorthCUA Harness provides full-lifecycle infrastructure for executing desktop and web tasks and turning each attempt into inspectable experience for learning. During execution, persistent workspace and retained task context let the agent build on earlier progress. We retain its execution record and resulting artifacts for outcome assessment, keeping the original environment available when live checks need to inspect the state the agent produced. Resources are released after the required inspection and record preservation are complete. By carrying each attempt through assessment and preservation, this lifecycle keeps decisions, outputs, and judgments connected to the same task attempt (Section 2). Figure 4 organizes this lifecycle at two levels. Within one task attempt, the unified agent runtime (01) supplies the shared interaction loop and platform tool interfaces. Long-horizon support (02) operates within this execution, keeping the next decision informed while retaining the complete trajectory. After acting ends, tool-using evaluator (03) checks the declared requirements using that trajectory and the live workspace. The Batch Rollout Service coordinates the parallel task lifecycles shown below. Each isolated environment proceeds through preparation, execution, and assessment. Centralized control and recording manage these attempts, keeping each workspace available through inspection and output capture. This distinction separates the mechanisms that make one attempt inspectable from the service that turns them into sustained experience production. Online RL reuses the execution and outcome interfaces under trainingside lifecycle management (Section 5.3), extending the same foundation from standalone collection to policy learning.

sections.title: 3.1 Unified Execution Across Desktop and Web
sections.content: Desktop and web agents follow the same basic loop: observe the software, choose an action, execute it, and use the feedback to continue. What differs is how each platform exposes its state and controls. Building on shared-runtime approaches to computer use (Zhang et al., 2026, Yan et al., 2025), we design Agent Kit to separate this common loop from platform-specific observation and action tools. Long-horizon support and evaluation reuse this same execution foundation.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Shared Agent Runtime
sections.content: We use shared runtime to organize interaction as ReAct-style loop with visual feedback (Yao et al., 2023). It assembles the request, observation, and relevant history into the next model input, invokes the policy, and executes the resulting tool calls. Returned observations and action results then inform the next decision. Common runtime services manage progress, budgets, NorthCUA Technical Report 7 / 123 NorthCUA 3.1 Unified Execution Across Desktop and Web Figure 4. NorthCUA Harness lifecycle. Within the expanded attempt, the shared runtime and long-horizon support sustain GUI interaction while retaining the full trajectory. The evaluator inspects recorded behavior and the live environment. Trajectory, task artifacts, evaluation results, and task metadata are saved in an experience record before the workspace is released. The lower lanes show parallel instances of this lifecycle, coordinated by the batch collection service. GUI scenes, agent imagery, and trajectories are illustrative. and termination, while environment-specific implementations supply the observations and operations. To build an agent for another platform, developers supply its perception functions, action tools, and observation processing hooks. The shared runtime then carries these components through the complete decision and recording loop, without rebuilding the agent flow. Section 3.1.3 details the desktop and web instances. CUA execution also involves several timescales. Application and browser sessions persist across actions, user request can require many decisions, and each decision produces feedback needed by the next. We represent these lifetimes through three nested scopes: Session maintains the agents execution state and associated software resources, such as browser session, across sequence of user requests. Round tracks the processing of one user request, including its multi-step execution, budget, and termination status. Step records one policy decision and the resulting tool execution and feedback. Each step can contain multiple tool calls. These runtime scopes organize interaction, while the task attempt supplies the collection-level identity used to associate actions, artifacts, and assessment. Each recorded action retains its request and session context, supporting task-level inspection and collection recovery. Session resources are managed within the broader environment lifecycle coordinated by the collection or training system. Appendix H.1 gives the execution-scope details. sections.title: 3.1.2 Tool Integration and Dispatch
sections.content: Desktop input, browser interaction, and workspace inspection expose different operations, whose implementations may run beside the agent or near remotely hosted application. To make these capabilities available to the shared decision loop, we use common tool interface that allows their implementations to evolve independently. Tool definitions describe operations and their arguments, while dispatch connects each call to its implementation and returns the result to the requesting step. The Agent Kit integrates local functions and tools exposed through Model Context Protocol (MCP), whose standard tool descriptions and invocation messages support capability discovery and execution (Model Context Protocol, 2025). Both paths feed the same interaction history and recording services. Platformspecific controls can therefore be added through tool bindings while reusing task progression and feedback handling. To reduce the repeated inference overhead of long GUI workflows, we allow the model to issue multiple action calls in single response. The runtime executes these calls serially in the specified order, allowing actions that can be planned together to share one model invocation. For computer use, tool feedback also needs to describe the state after an operation. Post-action observation hooks attach fresh screenshots or page observations to state-changing tool results, giving the next decision current view of the interface. Section 3.2.1 develops this action-aware feedback design. The same tool separation supports centralized agents operating remote devices, whose collection lifecycle is described in Section 3.4.

Its platform adapter manages the active application, foreground window, and input focus so that an action reaches the intended control. This supports workflows across application windows and files, with screenshots, action results, and output artifacts retained for later assessment. Appendix H.2.1 lists its actions and parameter schemas. Its adapter maintains the active tab, page state, and element references as navigation changes the interface. The resulting record includes page observations, action results, and browser artifacts. Appendix H.2.2 specifies the corresponding browser tools and argument constraints. The adapters handle these platform differences, while both agents reuse model invocation, request progression, context management, and trajectory recording. sections.title: 3.2 Sustaining Long-Horizon Interaction
sections.content: Long-horizon execution is central challenge in practical computer use. Real software work can require many fine-grained GUI operations across applications, files, and intermediate artifacts, with later actions depending on earlier discoveries and decisions (Yuan et al., 2026). Editing document may still require value read from spreadsheet and an output requirement encountered much earlier. Meanwhile, repeated visual observations and tool feedback enlarge the history supplied to each decision (Lu et al., 2026, Lv et al., 2026). Sustaining these workflows requires controlling context growth while keeping current state, earlier progress, and task-relevant knowledge available for continued action. We separate the decision context presented to the model from the complete execution record retained for inspection and learning. To keep later decisions informed within limited context budget, we design three complementary mechanisms: action-aware visual context for recent states and operations, task-preserving compaction for earlier progress and remaining work, and structured working memory for facts and decisions the agent chooses to retain. Figure 5 follows one invoice workflow across these mechanisms. The visual window shows the steps leading to export, the summary keeps export marked as pending, and an agent-written note carries the overdue total into the report. Each view supplies information needed for continued action without replacing the full execution record. NorthCUA Technical Report 10 / 123 NorthCUA 3.2 Sustaining Long-Horizon Interaction Figure 5. The visual window contains historical pre-action overlays and the latest clean tool-result image. Textual action and result history can outlast image eviction until compaction. Compaction summarizes earlier actions and results, omits old GUI locators, and preserves recent complete exchanges and the current GUI. sections.title: 3.2.1 Action-Aware Visual Context
sections.content: Repeated GUI interaction produces an image-heavy history whose size grows with the workflow (Lu et al., 2026). Its visual content serves two related purposes: the current screen guides the next action, and recent states help the agent interpret what it just did. The resulting screen alone can leave the location of preceding click or the path of drag unclear, particularly after window or page changes. Visual context therefore needs to preserve both current state and the spatial meaning of recent operations within limited image budget. We use sliding window to provide bounded visual history of up to recent frames, including the latest clean screenshot. Textual action and tool-result history survives image eviction, retaining longer account of the interaction until the text-history policy calls for compaction. To keep the newest frame current, post-action observation hooks supply fresh post-action feedback alongside state-changing tool results. The next policy invocation receives this screenshot directly, avoiding dedicated model turn solely to request the resulting screen. NorthCUA Technical Report 11 / 123 NorthCUA 3.2 Sustaining Long-Horizon Interaction Figure 6. Action-aware visual feedback. Matched crops show the historical pre-action view with its NorthCUA overlay (left) and the clean resulting state (right). 01 click opens the chart dialog. 02 drag moves video clip earlier on its track. 03 Scrolling reveals route details below. 04 text badge records the payload entered into the focused field. Screenshots come from interactive GUI mockups with generated scenery. Overlays use the unmodified runtime renderer. The input badge is enlarged below its historical view. To help the agent connect its previous operation with the change now visible on screen, we design complementary action view in the historical frames. Visual prompting work shows how spatial marks can make image regions easier to refer to (Yang et al., 2023). Our historical action overlays mark the corresponding pre-action image, using different cues for different operations. As shown in Figure 6, click marker locates the control that opens dialog, drag path links the clips old and new positions, and scroll cue identifies the direction in which the page moved. Text and key badges record operations that are less clear from spatial marker alone. Figure 6 pairs each annotated pre-action view with its clean resulting state to make the operation and observed change easy to compare. In the runtimes decision context, historical overlays identify recent operations, while the latest clean screenshot provides the current interface for the next decision. Replacing an earlier clean frame with an overlay changes the image history. The training-segment rule in Section 5.3.3 preserves the input seen before that change. This bounded visual history preserves both the spatial meaning of recent actions and the current interface state. The textual record continues to accumulate across these visual windows, creating the next context-management challenge.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Task-Preserving Context Compaction
sections.content: Bounding images leaves another source of context growth: assistant messages, reasoning, tool feedback, and intermediate task information accumulate throughout the workflow. Earlier constraints and discoveries may still be needed when this text approaches the models usable input budget. Context-management methods consolidate long histories to retain useful information NorthCUA Technical Report 12 / 123 NorthCUA 3.2 Sustaining Long-Horizon Interaction within finite prompts (Ye et al., 2026). We adapt this principle to computer use by designing taskpreserving compaction around three priorities. When older history needs to be summarized, we preserve the immediate actionfeedback context, retain task progress, and avoid carrying stale GUI locators into later decisions: Protect current interactions. The task request, latest GUI observation, and latest few steps remain protected. Assistant actions stay grouped with their tool results, and open exchanges remain intact until their responses arrive. This preserves the immediate action feedback context, including the current GUI observation whether it appears in user message or tool result. Summarize task progress. The summary organizes goals, constraints, supported facts, decisions, completed and failed work, current state, open items, and artifact references around task continuation. Desktop and web profiles instruct the summarizer to retain semantic software state and observed effects while condensing routine navigation. For example, an extracted spreadsheet value, its source file, and pending export requirement can therefore remain available after the navigation history is compressed. The instructions also distinguish issued actions, observed effects, and unresolved completion claims: an export command and an observed saved file represent different evidence about progress. Handle transient GUI locators. Coordinates and element references can become stale after page update or application switch. The summary-input projection filters these volatile fields, and the summary instructions exclude old locators from current executable state. The retained current observation remains available for grounding subsequent actions. Later compaction updates the existing summary with newly eligible history, with source references available for inspection. This gives continued work compact account of its dependencies while keeping the full execution record available for outcome assessment. Alongside this budget-triggered consolidation, the agent can actively preserve important information as it is discovered.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Structured Working Memory
sections.content: During long task, an agent encounters information with clear future value: figure read from another file, requirement for the final deliverable, an unsuccessful approach, or plan for remaining work. Assistant messages can mention these details in the chronological history, where their later visibility depends on history retention and summarization. Giving selected information an explicit working-memory representation lets the agent decide what to retain and revise during execution, following the broader principle of agent-controlled memory management (Packer et al., 2024). To let the agent preserve useful information when it discovers it, we design dedicated text-only note tool. The agent can call this tool proactively to record spreadsheet value before switching to document, or to preserve correction while revising an unsuccessful approach. The righthand panel of Figure 5 shows this transfer: note N1 records the overdue total from the workbook for later use in the report. Notes are stored independently of the history summary and can be presented in subsequent decision contexts. This complements compaction: summary consolidates accumulated work under budget pressure, while note explicitly preserves information the agent expects to use again. NorthCUA Technical Report 13 / 123 NorthCUA 3.3 Agentic Outcome Evaluation Notes serve three purposes: (i) retaining reusable knowledge and choices through facts, constraints, and decisions, (ii) recording lessons and risks through corrections and precautions, and (iii) tracking progress and unfinished work through checkpoints. This organization encourages concise entries with clear role in later decisions. As work progresses, replacement notes can supersede outdated entries. The memory service maintains them within the authorized task and session, then supplies budgeted view of active entries to prompt construction. corrected value or revised plan can therefore replace the corresponding obsolete item in working context, keeping remembered information aligned with the agents evolving understanding of the task. Together, these mechanisms keep the current screen, accumulated progress, and reusable knowledge available for continued action. The complete execution record connects these decisions to the resulting workspace, providing the evidence for outcome evaluation and subsequent training. Appendix H.1 gives the runtime settings, and Appendix E.1 and Section 5.3.3 describe their training interfaces. Appendix J.1 follows photo-delivery task in which payment constraint remains available from reconciliation through the final email.

sections.title: 3.3 Agentic Outcome Evaluation
sections.content: Selecting GUI trajectories for learning requires accurate outcome judgments across growing variety of tasks. Dedicated verifiers become diﬀicult to write and validate when correctness depends on content, presentation, or application-specific state (Rosset et al., 2026). We therefore use an adaptive evaluator that interprets the declared task requirements and gathers the evidence needed to assess the work. Figure 7 shows how recorded work and active inspection together support an evidence-linked assessment. We build the evaluator as an agent-as-a-judge (Zhuge et al., 2025), reusing Agent Kit tools. After the acting phase ends, it selectively retrieves saved records and artifacts and can inspect the original workspace using authorized shell, GUI, and browser tools. It adapts its inspection to each requirement and seeks further evidence when the available observations leave the outcome unclear. This combines reusable inspection capabilities with task-specific judgment, extending assessment to requirements that lack dedicated executable checks. Task-grounded rubrics guide this process, and multidimensional reports connect the findings to experience selection and failure analysis. In Figure 7s export example, the evaluator checks that the PDF exists and opens it to compare its contents with the source. This artifact inspection supplies the evidence for its final report. We require this report to associate each criterion-level judgment with its evidence, uncertainty, and evaluator operations.

sections.title: 3.3.1 Artifact and Live-State Inspection
sections.content: The evaluator receives the task request, assessment criteria, and compact view of the execution records. Requirements may concern an earlier action, final file, or state that is visible only inside an application. To reach these different forms of evidence, it uses two complementary tool groups: Recorded evidence. Retrieval tools expose selected steps, screenshots, tool results, and retained artifacts. They let the evaluator inspect relevant parts of long trajectory as questions arise, while the full record remains available outside its current context. E1 records an issued export, E2 establishes file presence, and E3 exposes PDF contents for comparison with the source workbook. Unresolved questions prompt further checks and can remain unresolved in the final report. Evidence-linked findings distinguish task fulfillment from execution assessment. GUI views, tool results, actions, and findings are illustrative. Generated document views are cropped, intermediate actor actions are omitted, and selected quality fields are shown without ratings. Live task state. Live tools inspect the original device or sandbox through fresh screenshots, read-only shell commands, and GUI or browser operations. Web probes can reuse the actors browser session, including its tabs and page state. This access makes environmentresident results available for checking while the workspace is still alive. Appendix H.2.3 lists the evaluators retrieval tools, authorized live interfaces, and report schema. The evaluator chooses between these sources according to the requirement under review, continuing its investigation when an observation leaves an important question open. This environment-aware approach is also studied in Shi et al. (2026). For document export, for example, recorded action can show that export was attempted, file check can establish whether an output exists, and an application inspection can reveal its rendered contents. Comparing these contents with the task inputs supports judgments about their correctness. Each observation answers different part of the acceptance question. Selective retrieval and live access thus connect the history of an operation to its actual result. To preserve attribution, the assessment protocol pairs pre-inspection terminal evidence with separate record of evaluator operations. Each judgment is linked to the submitted work and the observations used to assess it, making the investigation traceable to the original attempt. The rubric then connects this evidence to task fulfillment and execution quality. Appendix H.1 details the inspection and attribution protocol. sections.title: 3.3.2 Task-Grounded, Multidimensional Rubrics
sections.content: The value of GUI trajectory depends on both its result and the behavior it demonstrates. Successful attempts can contain unnecessary detours or unintended changes, while an attempt blocked late by the environment can contain useful completed subtasks. Data curation therefore needs answers to two complementary questions: (i) which task requirements were fulfilled, to establish what the trajectory accomplished, and (ii) how the agent performed the work, to assess the behavior available for learning. We therefore design the rubric to combine task-grounded acceptance criteria with multidimensional execution assessment (Rosset et al., 2026). For task fulfillment, the request and declared acceptance conditions define the intended outcome. The rubric expresses these obligations as specific, individually checkable questions. Export tasks may require the right contents, destination, and format. Explicitly required procedures also form part of acceptance. Request-derived criteria are generated before scoring the trajectory, with the original task requirements governing their interpretation. Assessing these obligations individually identifies complete, partial, and unresolved fulfillment, including which requested subtasks have supporting evidence. For execution assessment, the report records process quality, eﬀiciency, side effects, and failure diagnosis alongside judgment uncertainty. These dimensions explain the path taken to the result: repeated ineffective actions may reduce its value as demonstration, while successful recovery can provide useful behavior to study. Failure diagnosis distinguishes agent errors from environment blockers, and uncertainty identifies judgments that need further checking. Findings are linked to the relevant requirements and recorded steps so that their scope can be inspected. Table 2 summarizes the dimensions and their uses. Together, the rubric and execution report describe both the result achieved and the behavior that produced it. Their links to specific requirements and recorded steps make the judgments useful for selecting complete demonstrations, reviewing local segments, and analyzing recurring errors.

sections.title: 3.3.3 From Evaluation to Experience Selection
sections.content: We use the reports separate rubric scores to select data for different learning goals. Task fulfillment identifies completed work, while process quality, eﬀiciency, and side-effect assessments let us adjust selection thresholds for each data cohort. For example, cohort of concise successNorthCUA Technical Report 16 / 123 NorthCUA 3.4 Reliable Batch Rollout at Scale ful demonstrations can apply stricter eﬀiciency criteria, while cohort meant to teach recovery can retain useful corrections and exploration within successful attempts. At the trajectory level, these criteria select complete demonstrations. At the segment level, requirement-linked evidence can guide review of completed subtasks or recovery sequences, with the original decision context and local outcome kept alongside the behavior. Figure 7s report separates completion from execution quality so that these dimensions can be used together in selection. Section 5.1 applies the reports to trajectory curation, and Section 5.2 retains complete episodes for long-horizon SFT.

sections.title: 3.4 Reliable Batch Rollout at Scale
sections.content: The preceding mechanisms turn one task attempt into assessed experience. Producing large training corpus requires many such attempts to run in parallel, each with its own software state. Their preparation, GUI execution, evaluation, and recording take different amounts of time and consume different resources (Xie et al., 2024, Yuan et al., 2026). Simply launching more agents can therefore create backlog at another stage, while an interruption after execution can leave useful work without complete record. To support eﬀicient large-scale collection, we design Batch Rollout Service that coordinates the entire task lifecycle. Following the environment-lifecycle perspective also explored in Peng et al. (2026), we combine centralized agent control with isolated workspaces, prepare upcoming tasks alongside ongoing execution, and manage load and recovery through record delivery. Figure 8 shows the two relationships behind this design. Panel (a) connects one controller to independent device workers. Panel (b) shows how their lifecycles overlap: the same-time marker crosses evaluation, execution, and preparation in three different attempts. The service coordinates this concurrent work so that completed attempts produce usable experience records.

sections.title: 3.4.1 Remote Execution with Centralized Agent Control
sections.content: As collection grows, prompts, model settings, and agent logic continue to change. Placing that logic inside every task environment would require updating those environments whenever the agent changes. We therefore separate centralized agent control from device execution, as shown in Figure 8(a): Centralized controller. One service manages multiple agent runners and their device workers. It maintains prompts and agent configuration, assembles context, invokes the model, and dispatches actions. Device worker. Each worker runs inside one tasks isolated sandbox. It executes tool calls and captures observations from that environment. The worker starts with its sandbox and ends when the sandbox is released. The controller maintains long-lived WebSocket connection to each worker, sending actions and receiving observations over the same connection. Related distributed device orchestration appears in Zhang et al. (2025d). Here, each runner communicates with the worker assigned to its task, keeping the concurrent attempts separate. This division lets us update compatible prompt and model configurations centrally for later batches while reusing the same device-worker implementation and software templates. The device layer remains focused on observation and tool execution, so routine agent changes do NorthCUA Technical Report 17 / 123 NorthCUA 3.4 Reliable Batch Rollout at Scale Figure 8. Each worker shares its sandboxs lifecycle. (b) Staggered lifecycles overlap preparation, execution, and evaluation. Ready intervals mark prepared environments awaiting dispatch. Sandboxes remain available through live checks and output capture. Record icons mark captured outputs that persist after release. The vertical time slice marks concurrent stages. Timings and concurrency are schematic, and GUI scenes are generated illustrations. not require changing that layer. We save each batchs configuration for resumed collection and retain its trajectories on the controller side, where they survive sandbox release. With control and recording shared, scaling execution then depends on preparing enough independent task environments.

sections.title: 3.4.2 Isolated Environments with Pipelined Preparation
sections.content: A new attempt needs the files and software state specified by its task. Reusing workspace changed by an earlier attempt could alter those starting conditions (Xie et al., 2024). We therefore give each attempt its own initialized sandbox in our fresh-start collection mode. For Linux desktop and browser tasks, we choose E2B to create and manage these isolated environments (E2B, 2026b), with its desktop extension providing the graphical workspace (E2B, 2026a). Custom templates supply the operating system and shared applications, while per-task setup uploads files, launches applications, and prepares the required state. This lets tasks reuse software template without inheriting another attempts changes. NorthCUA Technical Report 18 / 123 NorthCUA 4 Experience Flywheel: Scaling Grounding and Agentic Experience Creating fresh environment takes time, so preparing tasks only when an agent is ready would leave collection waiting on setup. We address this with task-bound preparation queue: upcoming environments are prepared while earlier attempts are executing or being evaluated. Figure 8(b) makes this overlap visible in the offset Prepare blocks. Each ready workspace is assigned once to its matching task, provided enough time remains for execution and cleanup. It stays available through the required outcome checks and output capture, then is released. Preparation can thus run ahead without sacrificing fresh starting conditions or losing the evidence needed for assessment.

sections.title: 3.4.3 Completion-Oriented Scheduling and Recovery
sections.content: Preparation, execution, and evaluation progress at different rates. Independent admission can leave prepared environments waiting for execution or completed attempts waiting for evaluation. We coordinate admission with two controls. Stage-specific concurrency limits bound the number of attempts admitted to each stage. Because resource demand can vary within these limits, controller-pressure feedback slows new admissions when the shared controller remains busy. The first control limits local demand, while the second responds to load across the concurrent attempts. When connection is lost or downstream process fails, we first check whether the affected attempt is still running or has completed. Completed execution records can support retries of record-based evaluation or artifact processing, preserving the work already done. If the task itself needs to be rerun, we start it in fresh environment. Before delivery, we check that the required trajectory, observations, and assessments are complete and linked to the same attempt. Appendix H.3 gives the configuration and recovery details. Together, these designs carry the same runtime from individual task execution to sustained delivery of complete, inspectable experience. The Experience Flywheel in Section 4 builds on this foundation to construct tasks and curate the resulting records for model training.

sections.title: 4 Experience Flywheel: Scaling Grounding and Agentic Experience
sections.content: The NorthCUA Harness provides the execution infrastructure, but training computer-use model also requires large and varied supply of experience. The model needs examples of which control request refers to, as well as trajectories that show how successive decisions achieve complete goal. We design the Experience Flywheel to construct and curate these two levels of supervision. Single-step grounding pairs screenshot and query with the location of one visible control. End-to-end task construction supplies user goals, prepared workspaces, and outcome checks from which the harness can collect multi-step trajectories. These levels require different construction methods. For grounding, we start from visible controls and generate language that identifies them. For complete tasks, we connect available software and content, sourced requests, or verified seed tasks to the environments and assessments they need. This gives three complementary routes for scaling intents, environments, and verifiers. Executing the resulting tasks supplies experience for learning, although successful trajectories can remain scarce for the hardest workflows. We address that remaining gap through recursive exploration that retains useful skills and verified progress across attempts. Together, NorthCUA Technical Report 19 / 123 NorthCUA 4.1 Single-Step UI Grounding these methods supply localization examples and curated trajectories for the staged learning in Section 5.

sections.title: 4.1 Single-Step UI Grounding
sections.content: Single-step grounding takes screenshot and natural-language query, then predicts the location of the requested control (Cheng et al., 2024). Each training example contains screenshot, query that identifies visible control such as button or toolbar icon, and the controls coordinate in the original image. The main construction challenge is to write queries that identify the same control across different visual states and ways of describing an operation, especially in specialized applications (Lu et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025a). We construct these examples through two complementary routes: 1. Broad visual and structural coverage. We use screenshot evidence and available interface metadata to describe visible controls across diverse applications and states (Figure 9). 2. Documentation-grounded functional localization. We retrieve application knowledge when controls appearance leaves its function unclear, then use the matched function to generate queries (Figure 10). The first route expands interface and language coverage. The second fills gaps that visual evidence alone leaves unresolved. Both preserve the targets original location and produce the same screenshotquerycoordinate format, so their candidates can pass through shared quality and coverage checks.

sections.title: 4.1.1 Broad Visual and Structural Coverage
sections.content: To obtain broad grounding coverage, we first need screenshots of varied interfaces, then way to turn their visible controls into language targets. We use the three-step procedure in Figure 9. Panel (a) collects interface states, including states encountered during agent work. Panel (b) associates one visible control with its appearance and original location. This target record gives the query generator in (c) fixed referent: it can vary how the control is described while keeping the location label unchanged. To collect these states, we combine public UI datasets, web-collected GUI screenshots, and screenshots from agent trajectories, including real Linux desktop interaction. Trajectories contribute intermediate states such as open dialogs, expanded menus, and partially completed forms. We then use OmniParser, screen-parsing system that detects interactive regions and describes icons, to obtain candidate control boxes and descriptions (Lu et al., 2024). Accessibility annotations, when available for the same state, add control names and roles. These sources provide complementary evidence for identifying target. Visual parsing supports screenshots collected without accessibility metadata, while names and roles help connect visible controls to the language used in requests. For each target, we consolidate this evidence into one control record that keeps the crop and original image position together with the available name, role, color, appearance, and surrounding context (Zhang et al., 2026). For the calendar example in Figure 9(b), the record identifies the blue Week tab between Day and Month, together with point inside its clickable region. The full screenshot preserves the neighboring controls needed to make description specific. NorthCUA Technical Report 20 / 123 NorthCUA 4.1 Single-Step UI Grounding Figure 9. Constructing GUI grounding examples. (a) Screenshots cover public UI datasets, web-collected interfaces, and states encountered in agent trajectories. (b) Visual annotations and available accessibility metadata describe one target in its original screenshot. (c) Name-, position-, and operation-based queries each form separate candidate example with the same clean screenshot and absolute target point. The enlarged DayWeekMonth control group supplies the local evidence for these descriptions. GUI assets are illustrative. Target outlines explain construction, while training uses the unmarked 1536 1024 source image. With this record in place, we use an LLM to generate several queries from the record and full screenshot. The descriptions refer to the controls name, appearance, position, or an operation supported by the available evidence. In the example, Select the Week tab names the control directly, while Select week view expresses its purpose. Each query becomes separate candidate example paired with the clean original screenshot and the same coordinate. This variation broadens the language supervision without changing which control the model learns to locate (Chen et al., 2026a). This route supplies broad coverage of interfaces and visual states. When controls operation depends on application-specific knowledge, the documentation route provides the missing functional description.

sections.title: 4.1.2 Documentation-Grounded Functional Localization
sections.content: Some controls belong to specialized applications whose functions are hard to infer from screenshot alone. Parsing may locate toolbar icon while general-purpose LLM remains unsure what the icon does. This distinction matters when several visually similar controls perform different operations, as in layout editor with alignment controls for different parts of document (Wang et al., 2025c). NorthCUA Technical Report 21 / 123 NorthCUA 4.1 Single-Step UI Grounding Figure 10. Documentation-guided control disambiguation. (a) The screenshot supplies the application, version, and located target. (b) Online manual search retrieves control images and descriptions for visual top-k candidates. One aligns the left edges of separate objects, while the other aligns paragraph text within fixed text object. (c) Panel and selection context determine the function match, which guides query generation. Each query retains the original screenshot and target point. The GUI, documentation cards, and before/after operation diagrams are illustrative. Documentation supports sample construction. We design data-construction agent to supply the missing application knowledge before query generation. Figure 10 illustrates three steps. The agent identifies the application and target, then searches online documentation for candidate functions. It uses the surrounding GUI to select the function that fits the visible context. In the alignment example, the same-looking alignment symbol could refer to moving objects or formatting text. Matching its documented function resolves what query can reliably ask the agent to do with the already located control. Identify the application and target. This route begins with the same OmniParser-based screen parsing, which provides candidate control boxes and crops while preserving their locations in the original screenshot (Lu et al., 2024). Given the screenshot and target crop, the construction agent identifies the application and any visible version information, such as Inkscape 1.3 in panel (a). These details constrain the documentation search to the software in which the control appears, while the crop provides the visual target to match. Retrieve documented functions. Using that application identity, the agent searches online user guides and manuals and extracts illustrated controls with their function descriptions. We keep each illustration with its function description and page context, so that visually similar icon retains the information needed to interpret its operation. Image-embedding similarity then narrows these references to top-k candidates (Radford et al., 2021). Panel (b) shows both parts of this step: the online manual search and the candidate operations retrieved for the target icon. NorthCUA Technical Report 22 / 123 NorthCUA 4.1 Single-Step UI Grounding Match with GUI context and generate queries. Visual similarity supplies candidates but can leave the operation ambiguous. The agent therefore compares their descriptions with the full screenshot, neighboring controls, and active tool group. This contextual check matters because similar icons can denote different operations. In Figure 10, object alignment and paragraph alignment provide plausible visual candidates. Object alignment moves selected canvas objects to align their left edges, whereas paragraph alignment left-aligns the text within text object. The visible Align and Distribute panel identifies the relevant tool group, and the selected canvas objects provide complementary evidence for the object-alignment interpretation. The accepted match therefore links specific function description to the control already located in the screenshot. Once the function is resolved, we give the accepted description, target crop, and full screenshot to an LLM to generate query variants. One can request the documented operation, such as aligning selected objects along their left edges. Another can identify the same control through its tool group and appearance. All variants inherit the original target coordinate. Thus, application knowledge enriches the query while preserving the common grounding format. The documentation and retrieval candidates remain construction-side evidence, and the resulting samples enter the shared quality checks below.

sections.title: 4.1.3 Quality Control and Coverage
sections.content: Both routes produce the same candidate format: clean screenshot, query, and target coordinate. We use two complementary checks before adding sample to the corpus: Correctness check. Geometry checks confirm that the point lies inside the annotated control. Multimodal review then checks that the control supports the described operation, the query refers to it, and the description is unambiguous among nearby controls. Documentation-derived examples also carry their accepted function match into this review. Coverage check. Deduplication removes repeated screenshots and near-identical descriptions. Selection retains useful variation across applications, UI states, control types, and query styles, so that different ways of referring to control remain represented. These checks address different reasons larger candidate pool may fail to provide useful supervision: incorrect target labels and repetitive coverage. Geometry or identity failures return to construction when they can be repaired, while unresolved cases are excluded. Selection then retains accepted examples across interfaces and language styles. Appendix records the annotation, matching, and curation settings. The accepted examples enter mid-training as direct localization supervision. Screenshots acquired during multi-step collection can also enrich this pool with states encountered in actual software work. The next subsection extends the same construction logic from identifying one control to carrying out complete user goal. NorthCUA Technical Report 23 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Figure 11. Three task-construction routes. Scaling Environments prepares files and applications for sourced requests or reconstructs website interfaces and backing state from references. Scaling Verifiers jointly adapts requests, setup, and executable checks, then tests tasks and verifiers. Each alternative route produces complete task binding request, environment setup, and outcome assessment. GUI trials test completion from the initial state, while result probes test acceptance of correct outcomes and rejection of incorrect ones. GUI assets and task packages are illustrative.

sections.title: 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers
sections.content: Grounding examples teach the model to locate requested control. Learning to plan and act across complete workflow also requires interaction trajectories (Wang et al., 2025b, Jung et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026a). To collect them, we must turn each user goal into an executable task by providing the workspace it needs and reliable assessment of its outcome. Figure 11 compares three construction routes by what they start with and what they generate: Scaling Intents starts from applications, files, or website content and generates requests supported by their functions and facts. Scaling Environments starts from sourced requests or reference websites and builds the files, applications, or local website needed to execute tasks in that setting. Scaling Verifiers starts from tasks whose outcomes can be checked by reliable scripts. It generates related tasks by adapting the request, setup, and executable verifier together. GUI views, requested output layouts, abbreviated filenames, and the launch command are illustrative. Each column ends with complete task: request, workspace initialization, and outcome assessment. The routes thus expand task supply from different resources while retaining the same requirements for execution and checking. Depending on the task, assessment uses an executable verifier or evaluator inspection of the declared acceptance conditions. We package the output of each route in the same CaseSpec contract introduced in Section 2. Figure 12 shows one saved commercial-review task: its request asks for quarterly comparison, its workbook and startup instructions establish the initial Calc workspace, and its requirements specify the deliverables and how they should agree. The dashboard, memo, and review deck in Figure 12 are outputs the agent is asked to create. The post-run hook gathers available files for inspection against those requirements. This example shows what all three routes need to establish, even though they start from different resources. sections.title: 4.2.1 Scaling Intents
sections.content: Applications and working materials are readily available from software templates, public file collections, and websites. However, these resources do not come with varied set of natural user requests grounded in their contents and capabilities. We design Scaling Intents to generate such requests from the operations the software supports and the content already present. This grounding gives the requested work concrete subjects and feasible actions, while variation in goals and phrasing broadens the collection. We first describe desktop base tasks, then extend the construction to dependent long-horizon workflows and web content. Desktop base tasks. For desktop base task, we need to connect supported software operation to material on which it makes sense. Figure 13 illustrates the three steps used to generate the request. We first choose an application and one of its supported functions. That choice establishes the requirements for selecting compatible source file. The selected files content then supplies the facts from which an LLM writes grounded request. Once the request is defined, we prepare its starting workspace and assessment to form the complete task shown in the lower panel. NorthCUA Technical Report 26 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Select function. We begin with E2B templates that provide installed applications and their dependencies for oﬀice work, media, file management, browsing, and system settings. Each application has profile of supported operations and readable file formats. We choose the target application and an eligible operation according to the desired coverage of software and functions. Selecting Calc and filtering, for example, determines both what the eventual request will ask for and what kind of input it needs. Match file. To supply these inputs, we collect tens of thousands of files from public and open resources and supplement them with agent-generated materials (Ge et al., 2026). We index their formats and extract bounded content summaries, including spreadsheet fields and sample values or document text excerpts. With the function selected, we use its format and material requirements to find usable candidates. spreadsheet-filtering task needs readable workbook whose fields support meaningful selection condition. Sampling favors files used less often within the construction run, and the selected files summaries become inputs to request generation. For settings tasks, the relevant material is the application preference state instead of source file. Write the request. We give an LLM the selected function and file summaries, together with persona describing the users role and motivation (Jung et al., 2026). The function fixes the operation, and the summaries identify the concrete subjects, fields, and values to which it can be applied. For example, workbook summary that identifies Status column containing Pending supports request such as Filter the open spreadsheet to show only the pending records and save it. The filtering condition comes from the workbook, and the persona guides how the user expresses the need. Assemble CaseSpec. The request now describes feasible work, but the executing agent still needs the corresponding files and application state. To establish this starting point, we specify where the harness should place the selected files in the sandbox, which software template and dependencies to use, and which application or document to open before the first action. In the example, opening the workbook in Calc makes the open spreadsheet an unambiguous reference. Tasks involving several files instead identify them by name or workspace-relative path. The same requested change determines the completion criteria. The workbook should be saved with the pending-record filter applied and all source rows retained. Figure 13 uses matched views of the initial workbook and the required saved filter, which hides nonmatching rows without deleting them. The request, workbook, startup instructions, and required result form one CaseSpec. The same selection therefore supplies the content of the request, the file the agent operates on, and the result to inspect. Desktop long-horizon tasks. Base-task generation connects function to suitable content. Long-horizon construction extends these local matches into coherent workflow, especially across applications, by defining how later stages use information or results produced earlier (Yuan et al., 2026, Ge et al., 2026).
