We therefore plan the workflow before choosing its concrete materials and writing the request. The procedure in Figure 14 has three steps. First, we assemble work stages into dependency graph so that they contribute to shared goal. We then prepare the files and records that make each stage executable and its required outcome specific. Finally, we use this grounded plan to write the request and package the starting workspace and outcome requirements. The resulting task asks for coherent workflow whose operations are connected by shared purpose and explicit prerequisites. NorthCUA Technical Report 28 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Plan the workflow. We encode recurring workflows as scenario blueprints, each defining final deliverable, candidate stages, their applications and materials, and their prerequisites. For the oﬀice scenario, source review, delivery-record update, and final document all contribute to preparing the same delivery package. For each instance, target task length, application coverage, and desired interaction challenges guide the choice of blueprint and compatible stage combination. We favor less-used scenarios and components, then use seeded sampling among eligible combinations to vary the work. combination is retained when its prerequisites are present and every selected stage contributes, through its dependencies, to the overall workflow goal. Operation variants further specify the requested result, such as requiring the PDFs text to remain searchable. We represent the selected workflow as directed acyclic graph (DAG), planning abstraction also used for cross-device orchestration in UFO3 (Zhang et al., 2025d). Here the graph specifies the task-construction plan. Each node is work stage, such as inspecting document for approved content, and may require several GUI actions. Edges can express use of earlier information or artifacts, or required execution order. We retain the blueprints dependencies and, when constructing longer workflows, add precedence between selected stages that use shared facts. Figure 14(1) shows an oﬀice-delivery example of this planning process. The shared goal is to produce current delivery package and reconcile its business record. We organize that work into four stages. Source inspection (A) establishes the approved content, which guides the search for obsolete wording in an older deck (B). Record reconciliation (C) can begin independently. The final PDF stage (D) uses the findings from and B. The blueprint also places the record update before PDF production, shown by the dashed C-to-D edge. This edge specifies workflow order, while the updated record remains separate deliverable with its own check. Before preparing the materials, we check the assembled plan for cycles, missing prerequisites, and inconsistent production or use of files. The checked plan associates each stage with its application, required inputs, and expected output, so material preparation can follow the dependencies of the workflow. Ground the workflow in materials. The DAG specifies what each stage should accomplish, but its nodes still need concrete information to operate on. We ground each node by selecting or generating the files and service records required by that subtask. Existing-file selection follows the same principles as base-task selection, matching application support, file format, and content. Long-horizon construction also considers whether the selected files belong to shared project or directory and whether their contents support the relationships between stages. File summaries supply the names, values, and other details used to specify stage goals and acceptance conditions. When the workflow calls for generated materials, we instead choose scenario facts and place them in the files or records the agent will inspect. The oﬀice sample follows this path in Figure 14(2). The approved document supplies value that the final PDF should include, while the older deck contains obsolete wording that the PDF should exclude. The business record supplies the initial state for reconciliation update. Each material therefore has role in both the work stage and its outcome condition. The example requires two results: the PDF and the updated record. We check that the required information is available through the selected applications and that generated files contain their assigned content. Linking each requirement to its source and its NorthCUA Technical Report 29 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers later use keeps the workflow grounded across stages. The output is task plan with concrete input files, specified initial record values, stage goals, and corresponding outcome criteria. Create the executable task. With the work and its materials fixed, we use an LLM to write the user request. It receives the user-visible goal, references to the available materials, and required constraints, together with selected persona and expression style. These choices vary how users describe their work while preserving the constructed task. Facts designated for discovery remain in the workspace for the executing agent to find. The request can ask for reconciled delivery record and searchable PDF index without revealing the values or obsolete terms the agent needs to discover. Query checks compare the wording with the task plan, return inconsistencies for revision, and filter semantically duplicate requests. Figure 14(3) brings the request-writing, workspace, and assessment branches of the same grounded plan together. As in base-task construction, initialization instructions place the files and open the required applications. Here they also prepare the business record used by the workflow. Outcome assessment checks the requested PDF, record changes, and source preservation. Together with the request, these components form the CaseSpec executed by the harness. The DAG organizes task construction, while the executing agent plans its own GUI actions. The shared task plan keeps the goal, workspace, and assessment aligned as the collection expands to longer, multi-application workflows. Web tasks. An existing website supplies records and pages that can be read or changed through interface controls. We generate requests from this material in three steps. Examining the content and controls first establishes what work the site supports. We then select goal involving that content and ask an LLM to express it as user request. The chosen goal determines the initial records to prepare and the outcome to assess, completing the web task. We first identify the information visible on the relevant pages and the controls used to access or modify it. On an illustrative task-management site, these include task names, due dates, and status values, together with controls for filtering the task list, opening task, and changing its status. This combination supports requests to find tasks with particular properties and apply corresponding update. Using this account of the site, we select conditions that match records in the starting data and an operation available through the interface. We then use an LLM to express the grounded goal as user request, for example: Mark tasks due before 1 September 2026 that are still In progress as Needs follow-up. The due dates and current statuses determine which tasks qualify, and the status control provides the requested operation. Other requests use different items, conditions, and available actions to cover information retrieval, comparison, and form filling. The generated request determines which initial state to prepare and which result to assess. We record its entry page, startup instructions to open that page in the browser, and any setup needed to make the selected records available. In the example, the starting records establish which task identifiers satisfy the date and status conditions. Outcome assessment checks the updated status of those same tasks after execution. Keeping their identities tied to the starting data lets the check follow the requested items even after their status changes. Across desktop and web, these constructions turn available software and content into user requests with defined starting states and outcomes to assess. The resulting CaseSpec binds the goal and requirements to the selected resources and initialization instructions. The next route NorthCUA Technical Report 30 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers starts with an existing request or reference website and builds the workspace needed to support it.

sections.title: 4.2.2 Scaling Environments
sections.content: Scaling Intents uses the workspaces already available to generate new requests. Sourced requests offer complementary resource: they describe useful work, but often omit the files, dependencies, or application state needed to execute it. Reference websites and software issues likewise describe interactions without necessarily providing an isolated environment for collection. We design Scaling Environments to build these missing execution conditions. For desktop requests, this means preparing the files and applications assumed by the user. For Web tasks, we collect open-source frontends and reconstruct workflows from public URLs to create local environments that we can initialize and reuse. We also develop repository-based frontend testing as distinct web-agent application, where runnable project lets browser interaction test candidate code repair. Desktop environments. Forums contain user-reported software problems, while tutorials and help resources describe practical workflows and their intended results (Wang et al., 2025b). These sources provide goals grounded in software use, but their descriptions often assume attachments or workspace state that the collector does not have. We collect tens of thousands of such requests and task seeds from forums, wikiHow, and help resources. The construction problem is then to supply the inputs and startup conditions each seed assumes while preserving the work it asks the agent to do. We therefore design an environment-building agent, EnvAgent, to interpret each request and prepare its input files and startup plan. Figure 15 illustrates three construction steps. The agent first retrieves and reads candidate files to establish which requirements are already supported. Any missing inputs then guide file generation, using the retrieved material to keep related records consistent. With the inputs available, the agent specifies the request and startup plan and checks that they agree. failed check returns the affected input or instruction for revision before the package becomes CaseSpec. The order-comparison example below shows how the retrieved and generated materials contribute to the same task. Prepare the input materials. EnvAgent uses the request and selected software template to identify the applications and inputs the task needs. Comparing orders and shipments, for example, requires two tables that refer to the same orders, with shared identifier through which their records can be matched. request restricted to particular month also requires the corresponding date information. We reuse the indexed file formats and content summaries from Scaling Intents to locate candidates, using project and date information to find related tables. EnvAgent then reads their records to confirm that the identifiers refer to the same orders and that the files contain both shipped and outstanding orders for the comparison. If the retrieved materials meet the input requirements, the agent proceeds to request and startup specification. Otherwise, the unmet requirements guide generation. Figure 15(2) shows an example of this step. Given suitable order table but no matching shipment table, EnvAgent uses file tools and reusable construction skills to create shipment table with matching identifiers and business context. The resulting input set gives the requested comparison concrete files to operate on. NorthCUA Technical Report 31 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Figure 15. Request-driven desktop environment construction. EnvAgent identifies the required resources, retrieves an order table, and uses its identifiers to construct missing shipment table. An LLM grounds the sourced request in the prepared filenames and their shared Order ID field. EnvAgent specifies startup and checks the materials and preparation plan, revising inputs or instructions when checks fail before producing CaseSpec. The GUI agent subsequently performs the requested comparison. GUI views and records are illustrative. Specify and check the task environment. The files establish which names and fields the request can refer to. We use the original request and these file details to guide an LLMs replacement of general references with concrete ones, preserving the goal and constraints. In the example, the request now names the two workbooks and their shared Order ID field. It asks for unmatched orders in separate file and preserves any original source-protection or time restriction. The GUI agent still needs to identify the outstanding orders and create the result file. The refined request also determines how execution should begin. EnvAgent specifies that both inputs be placed in project directory, Calc be launched, and the order table be opened. The startup plan waits for the application window to be ready, with the shipment table available alongside the order table. These instructions give the harness the sequence needed to present the files and application assumed by the request. Before handoff, EnvAgent checks the prepared materials and startup plan. File tools establish whether the inputs exist and have valid formats, while the agent reviews whether their contents support the requested comparison, whether the template provides the required applications, and whether startup actions place the files before opening them. Findings such as missing identifier field or an incomplete startup action lead to revisions of the affected material or instruction. After file changes, EnvAgent submits new inspection report before finalization, so the report describes the materials that will actually be delivered. NorthCUA Technical Report 32 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers The checked request, files, environment configuration, and startup plan form the CaseSpec from which the harness creates the E2B instance and establishes the starting application state. With the input files in place, the GUI agent performs the comparison and saves missing_orders. xlsx, whose contents are then checked against the required orders alongside preservation of the source files. Construction checks thus establish the starting conditions, while outcome assessment evaluates the work performed from those conditions. Web environments. We collect Web frontends from open-source websites as starting points for local task environments. To extend this pool, we also reconstruct selected workflows from public reference URLs (Chae et al., 2026). These references provide realistic pages and interactions, while local control lets us initialize records, repeat attempts, and construct multiple tasks within the same site. Our URL-to-environment construction builds on WebAnything (Xie et al., 2026) and follows the four steps in Figure 16. We first explore the reference to identify the required pages and behavior. Those observations guide construction of local interface connected to backing state. Once it runs, browser tests check the interactions and return discrepancies for repair. We then restore the intended starting data and package the checked site for task collection. These steps turn an external example into an interactive environment with controlled initial conditions. The builder begins at the reference URL and explores the workflows selected for reconstruction, retrieving relevant pages and accessible frontend assets. For record editing, this covers the list page, detail view, editing controls, and navigation between them. An existing request can further focus the exploration. The resulting observations establish which pages the local site needs and what each interaction should do. We use these observations and accessible frontend assets to build the local pages. Their interactions also specify the backend behavior to reproduce. When the references backing data or implementation is unavailable, the builder creates local schema, initial records, and update logic for the observed workflow. In the record-editing example, the list and detail views refer to the same record, and saving an edit updates that record for subsequent visits. Linking the reconstructed controls to these state changes makes the workflow available for actual browser interaction. If construction raises questions about page or control, the builder returns to the reference site for targeted inspection before continuing the implementation. Once the local workflow is runnable, browser testing agent checks its visual correspondence with the reference and the effects of its controls. For the illustrated check, it opens record, edits and saves it, and refreshes the page to inspect the stored value. An unreachable detail page leads to navigation repair, while lost update leads to correction of the backend state change. After revision, the affected interactions are tested again. Figure 16(3) shows persistence test on record R17. The agent changes Delivery plan to Delivery plan v2, saves, and reloads. Seeing the edited title after reload provides the evidence for this particular check. These tests modify the records that future tasks will use. Before collection, we therefore restore the declared initial records and entry-page state, keeping construction-test edits separate from task setup. We package this starting state with the checked site for isolated E2B execution. Its content and tested functionality also support Scaling Intents, allowing the same environment to supply multiple user tasks. NorthCUA Technical Report 33 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Figure 16. Reconstructing interactive websites from references. The aligned GUI views follow record R17 from the reference site to the local implementation and reload test. Observed pages and interactions guide the interface and shared backing record. The test edits and saves the title, then reloads the record to check persistence. Discrepancies return to implementation for repair and retesting. The checked site is packaged with its declared initial records and runtime configuration, separately from construction-test edits. GUI states and URLs are illustrative. Repository-based frontend testing. Frontend testing is an important application of web agents because code that builds successfully can still behave incorrectly when user interacts with it (Yang et al., 2025). We therefore treat issue-driven testing as distinct setting for environment construction and experience collection. repository supplies the application, and its issue report specifies behavior that browser interaction can test. Figure 17 shows how browser testing guides successive code revisions. We first prepare runnable project and turn the issue into fixed test expectation. coding agent then revises and launches the application, making candidate repair available to the web agent. The web agent replays the reported interactions and compares their effects with the expectation. Finally, its action trace, screenshots, and verdict return to the coding agent in test report. This evidence directs the next repair while keeping every iteration focused on the same issue. Environment preparation begins with GitHub frontend repositories whose issues describe browser-reproducible behavior. The builder installs dependencies, starts the project, and prepares the pages and data involved in the issue. This makes the reported problem available for direct interaction and supplies the workspace in which repairs will be tested. NorthCUA Technical Report 34 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Figure 17. Browser interaction guides iterative code repair. (1) The issue fixes the expected behavior. (2) The Coding Agent inspects and edits the relevant implementation, then launches candidate application. (3) The Web Test Agent edits R17, saves the new title, and reloads the page. The stacked views show the new title after saving and the old title after reload, with cursor overlays marking interactions. test report returns this discrepancy, recorded actions, and screenshots to the Coding Agent for repair and retesting under the unchanged expectation. Generated GUI views, code, and test feedback are illustrative. The issue then defines what to check in this workspace. Its expected behavior supplies the coding agents repair objective and test list of browser actions and expected results for the web agent. For example, an issue may report that an edited page title appears to save but disappears after reload. The corresponding test changes the title, saves it, reloads the page, and checks NorthCUA Technical Report 35 / NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers that the new title remains. Both the code change and its assessment therefore address the same user-reported problem. The coding agent inspects the relevant implementation using the issue and any feedback from the previous browser test. It then changes the code and launches the revised application. These actions, illustrated by the editor views in Figure 17(2), supply runnable candidate whose behavior still needs to be tested. The web agent performs the test actions against that candidate and captures the resulting states. visible save confirmation establishes what the interface showed immediately after saving. Reloading tests whether the change persists. In the illustrated failure, the edited title appears after save but the old title returns after reload. The browser test report links these states to the actions that produced them and states the discrepancy directly. The stacked views in Figure 17(3) follow the same R17 record through editing, saving, and reloading. Because the edited title should persist, the observed old title identifies discrepancy for the coding agent to investigate. This feedback guides its next revision, which the web agent tests again through the running interface. The issues expected behavior remains fixed across iterations. This loop supplies GUI interaction trajectories and outcome feedback tied to real development requests, with evidence qualification and final acceptance detailed in Appendix F.1. Case study of responsive homepage repair. Figure 18 follows local Mercedes-Benz GLE SUV homepage built from supplied materials. The request called for responsive page with usable controls and navigation. Two defects emerged when the WebTestAgent followed button click over time and inspected the page at narrow width. In the first browser test (R1), the WebTestAgent clicked Learn more and waited. The transient notification disappeared, leaving no stable confirmation. Resizing the page to 320 px then exposed second defect, with text navigation covering the centered logo. The R1 report on the left links both findings to the actions and screenshots that exposed them, giving the Coding Agent two specific behaviors to repair. The central patch excerpts show how this feedback changed the code. For the first finding, the Coding Agent added an HTML confirmation element below the button and updated its text through the JavaScript click handler, so the response could remain visible. For the second, CSS rule hid the text links at widths up to 560 px while retaining the hamburger menu. This freed space around the logo while preserving navigation access. The matching numbers connect each reported defect to its corresponding patch. With the revised page running, the Coding Agent requested second browser test (R2). The WebTestAgent clicked the button again, waited three seconds, and changed the carousel slide. The inline confirmation remained visible. At 320 px, the links no longer covered the logo, the menu opened and closed, and the page had no horizontal overflow. Together with homepage visual check, these observations supported PASS on three selected items from R1s five-item checklist. The two reported defects were resolved in this targeted retest. Together, these routes expand environment supply from user requests, reference websites, and runnable software projects. Their prepared workspaces support experience collection, and reconstructed sites also feed new task generation through Scaling Intents. Tasks equipped with reliable executable verifiers offer further route to expansion: the next section uses their goals and outcome checks as seeds for additional task construction. NorthCUA Technical Report 36 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Figure 18. Bug-guided repair and targeted retesting. Desktop and narrow-screen tests produce one report, which guides both code changes before retesting. Screenshots are later replays of archived code, with subtitle line breaks cleaned for presentation. Overlays, report excerpts, and abbreviated patches are explanatory. R2 passed three selected checks, including homepage appearance, without repeating all five R1 items.

sections.title: 4.2.3 Scaling Verifiers
sections.content: Task datasets and manually authored cases provide user goals already paired with executable verifiers. reliable verifier makes the intended outcome explicit and supplies repeatable check on collected trajectories. Creating additional checks is costly, however, because each needs to match its task and distinguish correct results from plausible mistakes. We design Scaling Verifiers to expand this resource by adapting existing taskverifier pairs (Wang et al., 2026a, Lv et al., 2026). Figure 19 illustrates the construction and validation phases. We first use seeds goal and success conditions to construct related tasks, changing the request, initial state, and verifier together. The new pair then undergoes GUI execution trial and tests of the verifiers judgments. Their findings guide repairs before the pair enters collection. NorthCUA Technical Report 37 / 123 NorthCUA 4.2 Scaling Intents, Environments, and Verifiers Figure 19. Expanding tasks and their verifiers together. The agent extracts subtask, changes selection criterion, or joins approval with export, adapting completion and preservation checks to the new task. The lower composition example separates GUI execution trial from verifier tests on prepared outcomes. The verdict column gives the requirement-derived response for each probe. Testing checks whether the verifier returns it. The task lists, generated GUI views, and hypothetical judgments illustrate the construction procedure. The ellipsis omits intervening GUI actions, including export. Initial-state preparation and repair iterations are not shown. This joint treatment matters because changing requests selection criterion also changes which records the verifier should accept as updated and which it should require to remain intact. Expanding the work and its success conditions. The construction agent reads the seed request, initialization, and verifier to identify useful subgoals, their prerequisites, and the observable changes that establish success. subgoal can involve several GUI actions, such as editing document and exporting the result. We use these subgoals in three different ways. Decomposition extracts meaningful part of the seed task. Variation changes the condition or operation while retaining its basic structure. Composition connects subgoals into longer workflow, whose later work uses earlier results. The approval example in Figure 19 shows the effect of each choice on the requested work and the corresponding outcome checks. Decomposition turns meaningful part of the workflow into task of its own. Extracting record selection yields request to identify the qualifying records, an initial state containing the required data, and verifier for the returned selection and preservation of all records. Variation changes the materials, parameters, or operations. new selection criterion leads to new target set derived from the corresponding input records. The request and verifier are updated to express and assess that change. NorthCUA Technical Report 38 / 123 NorthCUA 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection Composition joins compatible subgoals through their inputs and outputs. Adding summary export to an approval task makes the approved identifiers the contents of the later file. The adapted verifier checks the updates, the exported summary, and preservation of the records the request protects. The added dependency can produce more demanding multi-stage task. Across these changes, the agent resolves the actual identifiers and file references used by the request, environment, and verifier. In the composition example, the targets established during selection remain the targets during assessment, even when the update changes field used for selection. Desktop compositions carry the same relationship through documents and intermediate files. Requirements that matter during stage are checked there, while final-state requirements are assessed at completion. Testing the task and its verifier. Each rewritten task undergoes two complementary checks before collection. GUI trial examines whether an agent can carry out the request from the prepared state. Verifier probes examine whether the checker judges known outcomes as the task requires. The lower part of Figure 19 keeps these two sources of evidence separate. For the execution trial, we run CUA from the declared initial state with the rewritten request. Its interaction and resulting state reveal problems such as missing inputs, unreachable controls, or instructions inconsistent with the workspace. These findings identify which setup or request needs repair. To test the verifier itself, we construct outcome probes whose expected verdicts follow from the request and starting data, then compare those verdicts with the verifiers outputs. In the approval-and-export example, complete result should pass, whereas an otherwise correct update without the required export should fail. Additional probes isolate incomplete updates, changes to protected records, and allowed alternative outputs. disagreement identifies checker rule to revise, even when the GUI task itself can be completed. We collect trial failures and verifier disagreements into construction report. Setup and instruction failures return to task construction, while incorrect verdicts return to the verifier. After the revision, we rerun the affected tests against the same intended requirements before admitting the pair to collection. Requirements that need contextual judgment use the evaluator in Section 3.3. This feedback loop keeps task expansion connected to executable conditions and meaningful outcome assessment. The three construction routes supply tasks to the shared collection service (Section 3.4). Executing these tasks produces trajectories and outcome assessments. Obtaining successful experience from the hardest tasks introduces the next challenge.

sections.title: 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection
sections.content: The routes in Section 4.2 supply executable tasks whose rollouts provide experience for learning. During collection, however, we encounter long and diﬀicult tasks that remain unsolved within the ordinary budget. Collecting demonstrations of sustained planning and recovery from these tasks requires addressing two recurring obstacles. Repeated attempts can lose useful discoveries and repeat ineffective procedures. late failure can also force new attempt to rebuild substantial earlier work. NorthCUA Technical Report 39 / 123 NorthCUA 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection We design two recursive self-improvement (RSI) pipelines for collecting experience from these tasks. Each carries forward the information needed to address one of these obstacles. Knowledge accumulation. Skill-guided recursive exploration turns trial-and-error findings into tested procedures that guide subsequent attempts (Figure 20). Progress accumulation. Milestone-guided trajectory search preserves completed work and resumes exploration from the corresponding software state and agent context (Figure 21). Both use feedback from earlier trials to shape later exploration (Zhu et al., 2026). They target tasks that pass construction checks but remain unsuccessful in ordinary collection. The original acceptance conditions stay fixed. We check the completed task before admitting an assisted trajectory as full-task demonstration. Milestone-guided collection can also retain verified subtask traces from attempts that leave the full task unfinished.

sections.title: 4.3.1 Skill-Guided Recursive Exploration
sections.content: Some GUI tasks require procedure that the agent has not discovered. The diﬀiculty may be an unfamiliar application command, hidden prerequisite, or sequence whose useful effect becomes clear only after trying it and inspecting the result. Repeated attempts can make partial discoveries, but those discoveries remain scattered across their histories unless the collector carries them forward. We therefore need way to turn trial-and-error experience into reusable operating guidance. We design skill-guided loop with four stages, shown in Figure 20. Task-directed exploration first produces observations about useful operations and unresolved obstacles. skill creator then reviews that experience and consolidates actionable findings into written guidance. separate agent tests the candidate instructions before they are supplied to new task attempt. That attempt can use the validated procedure to make further progress, and its new discoveries feed the next round of skill refinement. The loop accumulates tested knowledge across attempts while retaining full-task verification for the final result. Explore the task and identify obstacles. We use computer-use agent to attempt the original query in its prepared workspace. It inspects the relevant applications and files, tries controls, and adjusts its action sequence as it observes their effects. An unsuccessful attempt can still reveal an important prerequisite, an ineffective action to avoid, or way to reach previously inaccessible state. Successful operations likewise show procedures worth retaining. We examine these findings in the trajectory and result, using evaluator observations of the live state to help identify the remaining obstacle (Section 3.3) (Shinn et al., 2023). In the representative report workflow in Figure 20, exploration may reveal several export options. One trial produces PDF with all the required pages but represents their text as an image. The searchability check then focuses further trials on which export settings preserve text. The initial exploration has thus turned broad completion goal into specific procedural question that can be tested in the application. Consolidate candidate skill. The skill creator reviews the accumulated trajectories and their outcomes. When the useful procedure is still unclear, further exploration or focused practice tests alternative operations. The creator turns the resulting findings into textual guidance that states when the procedure applies, which actions to take, and how to check its intended effect NorthCUA Technical Report 40 / 123 NorthCUA 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection Figure 20. Accumulating operating knowledge through exploration. The source report contains Quarterly, but an image-only export makes the phrase unsearchable in the PDF. Further exploration yields text-preserving procedure. An agent follows its fixed instructions in separate trial and searches the resulting PDF. The validated skill then guides new attempt in the original workspace, where full-task checks determine trajectory acceptance. The return arrow depicts failed task attempt, while failed validation also prompts revision. Accepted trajectories retain the supplied skill in context. GUI scenes, controls, actions, and outcomes are illustrative, with intermediate exploratory trials omitted. (Wang et al., 2024, 2026c). For the PDF example, this means recording the text-preserving export settings and search check, together with the image-only choice to avoid. The candidate gives later attempts concrete procedure and the relevant pitfall. Validate the skill independently. Guidance inferred from exploratory trials may omit prerequisite or misidentify why an operation worked. We therefore freeze the candidate and give it to separate agent in an independent validation trial. The agent applies the instructions and checks their claimed effect in the environment. In the PDF example, it exports using the specified settings and searches for phrase from the source document. Finding the phrase establishes the intended effect of this skill, while failed NorthCUA Technical Report 41 / 123 NorthCUA 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection check returns the instructions to exploration and revision. The revised candidate is tested again before admission for reuse. Reuse the skill and continue exploration. We provide the validated guidance to new attempt at the original task. The agent can now use the tested procedure when it reaches the relevant operation. If it encounters another obstacle, or discovers useful way to complete later stage, that experience feeds the same consolidation and validation loop. Previously validated skills remain available, so each round can build on what earlier attempts established. The process continues until an attempt satisfies the original tasks full acceptance conditions or the exploration budget is exhausted. Accepted attempts supply trajectories with the actual guidance retained in their decision context. The skill library also makes tested procedure available to later tasks that meet its applicability conditions. This accumulation is designed to improve hard-task collection by carrying useful knowledge between attempts. The TERRA dashboard case in Section 4.3.3 follows how charting problem becomes revised guidance that fresh attempt applies (Figure 22). For long workflow, however, even better-informed attempt can spend substantial effort repeating earlier work. The next pipeline addresses that remaining cost by retaining execution progress.

sections.title: 4.3.2 Milestone-Guided Trajectory Search
sections.content: A long task can be diﬀicult to finish in single attempt even when its individual stages are within the agents reach. When late failure ends an attempt, restarting from the initial state repeats work already completed. This motivates second RSI strategy in which collection focuses on smaller, verifiable goals and retains the work that reaches them. We design milestone-guided trajectory search to implement this strategy. We first decompose the original task into dependent milestones and their checks. GUI attempts then work toward one milestone at time, saving the workspace and agent context when check passes. Further attempts restore that checkpoint to explore the next stage, following the principle of returning to useful states for exploration (Ecoffet et al., 2021). After the final milestone, the original verifier checks the complete result before the selected path becomes full-task demonstration. Figure 21 illustrates how this process builds successful continuations on retained progress. It reduces the work each trial needs to repeat while keeping acceptance tied to the original task. construction case in Section 4.3.3 follows this accumulation of progress from an empty Blender scene to complete collected trajectory (Figure 23). Define milestones and their checks. We use planning agent to read the user request and the original verifier code, identify dependencies, and propose meaningful intermediate goals. Each milestone pairs subtask with check on its observable result. The goal should represent useful progress and leave state from which later work can continue. Reviewing the pairs against the original requirements ensures that local checks support the intended full task. This uses the decomposition principle in Section 4.2.3, here to guide collection within one long task. For the oﬀice workflow in Figure 21, the original goal includes updating business record and producing searchable PDF. We organize it into three milestones: complete the record update (M1), prepare the report (M2), and export the searchable PDF (M3). Their checks inspect the corresponding records, document content, and output file. The executing agent receives the permitted subtask guidance, while private verifier constants remain in the checking context. NorthCUA Technical Report 42 / NorthCUA 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection Figure 21. Retaining progress for branching trajectory search. Checkpoint M2 pairs the prepared report and software state with the agent context. Independent continuations restore this checkpoint to try different exports. The example contrasts image-only, text-preserving, and incomplete single-page exports. The lower panel retains the common prefix and the chosen continuation as one candidate path. The original task verifier checks the PDF, earlier record update, and source preservation before accepting the trajectory. Failed continuations leave the parent available for further attempts. GUI states and diagnostic outcomes are illustrative. Preserve progress and explore continuations. The harness supplies the first subtask to computer-use agent in the initial workspace and runs repeated attempts within the collection budget. When an attempt passes the milestone check, we save an E2B workspace snapshot together with the agent context about completed work, useful findings, and remaining goals. Restoring both gives the next attempt consistent starting point for the following milestone (Section 3.2). We retain the full interaction prefix alongside the bounded decision context and can keep several passing states to support different continuations. Retained checkpoints form the nodes of search tree, and GUI action sequences toward the next milestone form its branches. Each continuation restores its parent checkpoint in an isolated instance, observes the interface, and attempts the next stage. Passing results become checkpoints for the next milestone. If continuation stalls or fails its check, its parent remains available so that new attempt can try different sequence without replaying the earlier stages. NorthCUA Technical Report 43 / 123 NorthCUA 4.3 Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection We can also retain selected recoverable failed states for further exploration. These states keep their unresolved milestone labels. continuation attempts the necessary correction before advancing to later goals, allowing the collected path to include genuine recovery from an earlier mistake. Thus the tree can support both alternative attempts from verified progress and recovery attempts from useful but incomplete state. In Figure 21, branches and fail the export requirement, while produces searchable PDF. All three begin at M2, retaining the same earlier record update and report preparation. failed export can also trigger the skill exploration described above, whose validated guidance can be used by new continuation. The saved checkpoint preserves the work already done, and the skill helps the agent choose how to perform the unresolved operation. Verify outcomes and retain useful traces. After the final milestone, the original task verifier assesses candidate completions against all requirements, including those established in earlier stages. For the oﬀice task, it checks the PDF, the required record update, and source preservation. Search continues until branch passes this final check or the budget is exhausted. passing branch yields search-assisted trajectory: the actual parentchild path from the initial state to completion, combining its retained prefix with the selected continuations. It keeps the paths observations, actions, and supplied guidance, including mistakes followed by recovery. Failed sibling branches remain exploration records and are not spliced into the accepted trajectory. If an attempt completes only part of the milestone sequence, we retain only the trace portions associated with passed milestones as subtask-level demonstrations, preserving their original decision context. This recovers useful supervision from unfinished attempts and makes fuller use of the collection budget.

sections.title: 4.3.3 Case Studies of Knowledge and Progress Accumulation
sections.content: We use two case studies to explain how the RSI strategies collect experience on diﬀicult tasks. The first follows skill refinement while building live retail dashboard in Calc. The second follows milestone accumulation while constructing greenhouse cafe in Blender. In each case, the recorded attempts show what goes wrong and how retaining knowledge or progress helps subsequent attempts complete the task. Knowledge accumulation in dashboard task. Figure 22 starts with request to build quarterly operations dashboard for TERRA from sales records and store targets. The deliverables are an editable workbook with live calculations and charts, and matching one-page PDF. The request specifies grouped vertical columns and navy, teal, and orange palette. The diﬀiculty is translating these visual requirements into Calcs orientation and color settings, whose effects need to be checked in the saved workbook and exported PDF. In Attempt 1, the agent follows skill v1, which asks for grouped columns and final document inspection. These instructions leave the relevant API settings unspecified. The agent sets Vertical=True through the legacy chart interface, producing the horizontal bars shown in the top row. It discovers the correct setting and fixes the direction during this attempt, but the charts retain the default blue and red series colors. The final palette check therefore rejects the delivery. Reviewing this trajectory identifies the two changes shown in the middle of the figure. sections.title: 5 Staged Learning from Scalable GUI Experience
sections.content: The Experience Library assembled by the Experience Flywheel provides quality-selected demonstrations of software work, alongside grounding examples and executable tasks for further collection (Section 4). The next step is to turn these resources into policy that can reason about interfaces and carry out user goals across desktop and web applications. We design three-stage learning pipeline that develops this capability progressively, as outlined in Figure 2. 1. Broad GUI mid-training first establishes familiarity with controls, application functions, and their effects through diverse software experience. 2. Verified long-horizon SFT builds on that foundation and concentrates learning on highquality demonstrations that carry dependent work to completion. 3. Joint desktopweb agentic reinforcement learning then lets the policy learn from its own decisions and their outcomes in interactive environments. Each stage uses the preceding policy as its starting point while changing the learning emphasis, from operational breadth to sustained completion and then outcome-driven improvement. Table 3 summarizes the resources and priorities of the three stages. The shared interfaces of the NorthCUA Harness connect demonstration collection with online execution, so the policy can continue using the same observation and action conventions as training progresses. We describe each stage below. Appendix defines the supervised prediction units and how recorded RL attempts become learning samples. sections.title: 5.1 Broad GUI Mid-Training
sections.content: Computer-use agents encounter many applications, interface layouts, and ways of performing similar operations. To work across these settings, policy needs experience recognizing controls, interpreting their functions, and observing how actions change software state. We use broad GUI mid-training to build this foundation from diverse demonstrations (Wang et al., 2025c, Jung et al., 2026). Through the collection routes in the Experience Flywheel, the reported broad task corpus contains over 100,000 trajectories and over 4 million GUI interaction steps, spanning dozens of applications and hundreds of operation families. This range exposes the policy to different tasks, materials, and interfaces within and across applications. We complement the trajectories with approximately 40,000 single-step grounding examples to train spatial recognition and control localization directly. The following collection and selection choices determine what experience enters this mixture. Broad software coverage. We select commonly used desktop applications and organize their functions into operation families. These profiles guide the task requests and CaseSpec environments used for experience collection, making it possible to vary the operations demonstrated within each application. Sampling across applications and operations, together with variation in source files and user goals, broadens this coverage. Representative coverage in the application profiles and workflow templates includes: Oﬀice work. Calc tasks cover formulas, auditing and reconciliation, filtering, pivot tables, and print layout. Writer adds document formatting and annotation, while Impress covers slide composition, content insertion, styling, and synthesis of source material into presentations. GIMP tasks include cropping, resizing, annotation, and export. Inkscape adds vector text, color, alignment, and grouping operations. Image viewers, PDF viewers, and VLC provide content inspection and playback tasks. Workspace and information management. File-manager tasks cover organization and batch processing. Thunderbird, browsers, and VS Code add message handling, browser configuration, information lookup, and GUI-based file editing. CAD and 3D workflows. Expanded workflow templates define model review and part design in FreeCAD and SolveSpace, together with scene organization in Blender. Medical-image and anatomy visualization. 3D Slicer scenarios cover inspecting image volumes, checking orientation, annotating landmarks, and saving review scenes. To extend this coverage beyond individual functions, we also use the long-workflow construction in Section 4.2.1. Its dependent tasks provide experience combining operations, carrying information between applications, and maintaining progress toward shared deliverable. Midtraining therefore includes sustained workflows as part of its broad foundation, before the next stage concentrates on selected verified examples. We further enrich web experience with (1) information retrieval, (2) form filling, (3) humanverification flows, and (4) frontend testing. Retrieval and form filling represent common everyday uses of websites. Human-verification flows add visually conditioned interactions encountered during web use, while frontend testing exercises the effects of controls and the persistence of state changes. Together, these settings diversify both what users ask and how an agent must interact, complementing desktop operation with web-specific workflows. The web scenario library also provides browser-game and sliding-puzzle tasks. Grounding examples add direct practice locating the requested control, including specialized controls handled by the documentation-guided route in Section 4.1. Table 4 summarizes the coverage of these sources, while Appendix gives their rounded counts by domain. Outcome-based trajectory curation. Broad coverage is useful for learning only when the collected behavior provides worthwhile demonstration. Large-scale attempts can also leave tasks incomplete or spend many actions without progress. We therefore use the agent-as-a-judge evaluator in Section 3.3 to inspect each candidates requested outcome, trajectory, and resulting artifacts or state (Zhuge et al., 2025). Its assessment selects completed work with useful execution behavior for the training corpus. This selection limits the inclusion of incomplete or low-quality traces while preserving examples of successful software use across the coverage pool. Among the trajectories that pass review, selection preserves broad application and operation coverage. Meaningful exploration and recovery remain part of this experience when they lead NorthCUA Technical Report 49 / 123 NorthCUA 5.2 Verified Long-Horizon SFT to completed work, giving the model examples of how actions and subsequent observations inform the next decision. Outcome-based filtering thus makes quality control part of building large and varied training corpus. Learning localization, interaction, and assessment. The selected mixture teaches both where to act and how to continue task. For grounding examples, the model predicts the target controls coordinates from the request and screenshot (Cheng et al., 2024, Lu et al., 2024). Trajectories train the model to predict each recorded assistant response from the task and the observations and history available at that decision. Targets include recorded reasoning, text responses, and action tool calls, while screenshots and tool results provide context. This response-level objective connects interpreting the interface, deciding what to do, and issuing the operation. We also include evaluator trajectories as separate judgment-task source. These examples condition the model on the evaluators inspection context and train its recorded assessment responses, providing demonstrations of how to check an outcome and support judgment with evidence. Actor demonstrations retain their original decision-time context, separate from these evaluation inputs. The evaluator therefore serves two distinct purposes in mid-training: its reports select task demonstrations, and its own trajectories teach assessment. Appendix E.1 distinguishes the sample types and their response targets. Through this broad mixture, mid-training develops familiarity with diverse GUI functions, action effects, and ways of interpreting results. This provides the operational foundation for learning more demanding workflows. The next stage sharpens that foundation using concentrated set of high-quality, verified long-horizon demonstrations.

sections.title: 5.2 Verified Long-Horizon SFT
sections.content: Mid-training gives the policy broad experience operating software, including extended workflows. Sustaining correct work over long and diﬀicult task requires more concentrated learning signal: later decisions need to use earlier findings, preserve constraints, and complete the final deliverable. We therefore continue from the mid-trained checkpoint with supervised finetuning on selected long-horizon trajectories whose complete outcomes pass executable task verifiers (Yuan et al., 2026, Lu et al., 2026). The cohort contains approximately 3,000 trajectories and 310,000 GUI interaction steps. Selecting verified demonstrations. We start with tasks and executable checks supplied by Scaling Verifiers (Section 4.2.3) and collect successful completions. For diﬀicult tasks that ordinary attempts do not solve, the skill-guided and milestone-guided RSI routes in Section 4.3 provide additional ways to obtain candidate demonstrations. Skills carry useful operating knowledge between attempts, while retained checkpoints let exploration build on completed intermediate work. In either route, candidate enters this stage only after its final result passes the original task verifier. Appendix lists the source contributions that remain to be reported separately from this aggregate cohort. Within this accepted pool, we prioritize diﬀicult workflows with long-range dependencies while maintaining application diversity. We use length to identify sustained work, then inspect how later actions use earlier results to assess its dependencies. We then check whether these demonstrations provide usable training sequences. Data cleaning rejects unusable records and traces with malformed or unmatched tool calls or unproductive loops. This screening retains coherent NorthCUA Technical Report 50 / 123 NorthCUA 5.3 Joint DesktopWeb Agentic Reinforcement Learning recovery when the trace shows an error, its correction, and verified completion. Each retained trace keeps its original actionobservation sequence, preserving the context needed to learn that recovery. These checks combine programmatic outcome acceptance with demonstrations of purposeful work across stages. Learning sustained completion. With this selected corpus, we fine-tune the mid-trained policy to predict the recorded assistant responses from the request and decision-time context. The objective remains response prediction, but the data now emphasize maintaining task state, using intermediate results, coordinating work across applications, and recovering without losing the original goal. For assisted demonstrations, any supplied skill or milestone guidance remains in the context under which the recorded response was produced. Representation and sampling requirements are described in Appendix E.1. This stage strengthens sustained task execution on top of the broad operational foundation. The resulting policy is the starting point for autonomous rollouts, where its own choices can create states absent from the demonstrations. Reinforcement learning provides the next learning signal by connecting those choices to their task outcomes.

sections.title: 5.3 Joint Desktop–Web Agentic Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: Mid-training and long-horizon SFT provide policy that can recognize interfaces and follow demonstrated workflows. To develop its ability further, we let it learn from autonomous interaction. Its own choices determine which states it encounters, and task outcomes provide feedback on whether those choices accomplish the users goal. We use agentic reinforcement learning to connect this fresh experience to policy improvement (Qi et al., 2025, Lai et al., 2026). We train single policy jointly on desktop and web tasks. The shared runtime in the NorthCUA Harness already expresses both as repeated observation, reasoning, and tool-based action, making it natural to learn from them through one training loop. Platform-specific observations and tools retain the differences needed to operate each interface. Task-specific verifiers then provide outcome feedback for the work performed in either domain. Figure 24 follows an attempt from task preparation to policy update. The Task and Environment Manager selects executable cases and prepares their isolated workspaces and verifiers, giving NorthCUA Rollout Workers the conditions needed to act with the current policy. Once those attempts have been recorded and scored, the Experience Adapter pairs the model calls with their task outcomes to construct training samples. These task-grouped samples let the Policy Learner compare alternative attempts with GRPO and update the shared policy (Shao et al., 2024, Zhu et al., 2025). Returning the new weights to the workers closes the loop, so subsequent interaction uses the updated model. The following subsections explain how we select useful tasks, obtain comparable feedback, and preserve executed decisions as that feedback enters learning.

sections.title: 5.3.1 Selecting Tasks with Outcome Variation
sections.content: GRPO obtains its task-level learning signal by comparing the rewards of multiple attempts at the same task. An attempts relative outcome determines its advantage within that group. If all valid attempts receive the same terminal reward, their terminal group-relative advantages are zero. Since GUI rollouts are costly, we first identify tasks on which the SFT policy produces different outcomes, so initial collection can provide informative comparisons. sections.title: 5.3.2 Joint Rollout and Task-Relative Feedback
sections.content: With the task pool selected, we generate fresh attempts and turn their outcomes into the comparisons used by GRPO. For each case, the manager first establishes equivalent starting conditions. Workers then act in those environments, and the task verifier assesses each completed attempt. The recorded decisions and outcome are converted into samples for policy learning. The Task and Environment Manager prepares separate E2B sandbox for each attempt in task group. All members receive the same request, initial files and application state, verifier, and NorthCUA Technical Report 52 / 123 NorthCUA 5.3 Joint DesktopWeb Agentic Reinforcement Learning execution budget. Their sandboxes are isolated, so one attempts edits do not change anothers starting conditions. This makes differences in outcomes interpretable as alternative executions of the same task. NorthCUA Rollout Workers use the policy to carry out each multi-turn attempt. Desktop and web execution follow the same runtime loop, using their respective screen or browser observations and allowed tools. After execution, the manager runs the task verifier on the resulting workspace. Its valid verdict supplies the complete attempts terminal reward. Both successful and unsuccessful attempts contribute to the comparison, while setup or evaluation errors follow the separate invalid-attempt path. The Experience Adapter binds each outcome to the model calls from that attempt. It reconstructs training samples from the recorded multimodal inputs and responses, retains behavior-policy likelihoods and versions, and marks which response tokens are learning targets. Each sample keeps its task and attempt identity so that the Policy Learner can compute relative advantages within the correct task group and apply the GRPO update. Desktop and web groups contribute to the same shared policy through this procedure. This completes the path from an executable case to outcome-driven learning. For long GUI attempts, however, converting the record into training samples requires additional care. The next subsection explains the two rules we use to preserve both the original decision conditions and the attempts learning contribution during that conversion.

sections.title: 5.3.3 Preserving Executed Decisions for Learning
sections.content: The rollout procedure provides complete attempts and their outcomes, but the learner must also preserve the conditions under which each decision was made. Our harness maintains sliding window of recent screenshots and can compact earlier history. As task proceeds, an image may leave the window or summary may replace earlier messages. Using only the final history to train every response would therefore change the evidence available to some decisions. Preserving the sampled input is also central concern in harnessed agentic RL (He et al., 2026). To accommodate this context management, we design the Experience Adapter around two preservation rules. First, each response is learned with its recorded decision-time input, starting new training segment when the history no longer extends consistently. Second, those segments retain the reward attribution and learning weight of their original complete attempt. This matters because frequent context changes can split one attempt into more segments than another. Figure 25 illustrates input preservation in panel (a) and attempt-level comparison and aggregation in panel (b). Together, the two rules let the harness manage long histories without turning representation change into different learning problem. Preserve decision-time inputs. Training associates each response with the context that produced it. To preserve this association through context changes, we capture each model calls input, delivered response, generation log-probabilities, and behavior-policy version. The adapter joins consecutive calls only when their text and ordered image histories form confirmed prefix extension under the same version. Image identity includes its content digest, so replacing clean frame with the historical action overlay from Section 3.2.1 also breaks this prefix. The adapter starts new segment from the captured input whenever images are replaced or evicted, summary rewrites history, or the behavior version changes. sections.title: 5.3.4 Continuous Rollout and Policy Updates
sections.content: Training from long GUI rollouts is costly even after the samples are correctly constructed. Overlapping screenshot windows repeat visual preprocessing and carry large tensors to the learner. Meanwhile, task durations vary, so waiting for every active task before updating the policy can delay the next learning cycle. We address these two costs separately: visual-delivery mechanisms reduce redundant input preparation and transfer, while asynchronous coordination lets policy updates proceed without restarting ongoing tasks. Deliver visual experience eﬀiciently. Adjacent decision windows often contain unchanged screenshots. Processing every window from scratch repeats work on those images. For supported per-image processor, the Experience Adapter therefore reuses the preprocessing tensors of unchanged images within an attempt and processes only new images. It reconstructs the requested image order under the same processor settings. Changed images or settings require fresh processing. The reuse saves CPU preprocessing while retaining every image in the model input. The neural visual encoder still processes the complete visual input. Large image tensors also add delivery cost after preprocessing. The object-store path supports lossless tensor compression, retaining compressed payload only when it is smaller. The learner decodes the microbatch it is about to consume, recovering the same values, shape, and type. Bounded CPU workers prepare samples, and group admission counts completed work awaiting delivery so that preparation does not create an unaccounted queue. These mechanisms target redundant processing and payload transfer while preserving the samples contents. Appendix E.4 describes the implemented reuse and transport paths, their configuration, and the checks used to assess sample equivalence and delivery cost. Coordinate policy updates asynchronously. In asynchronous mode, completed groups can supply the learner while other workspaces remain active. To publish an update, the system pauses new model calls, waits for calls already in progress, commits the new weights, and resumes calls. Ongoing tasks keep their workspace and completed work, so later decisions can use the updated policy. For attempts spanning several versions, the clipped objective is an offpolicy approximation. Preserving the recorded inputs keeps the sampled decisions identifiable, while policy lag affects the resulting update. Appendix E.2 defines policy lag and mixed-version attempts and distinguishes asynchronous coordination from synchronous collection. This coordination lets learning continue while ongoing tasks retain their environments and completed work. Together, these mechanisms address the cost of supplying visual experience and coordinating updates, while the preceding preservation rules keep learning tied to the executed decisions and complete task outcomes. sections.title: 6 Experiments and Analysis
sections.content: Our evaluation follows the progression from identifying control to completing software task. We first compare grounding, desktop, and Web performance, then examine how results change through long-horizon SFT and joint desktopWeb RL. Trace analyses and selected cases connect these scores to concrete decisions, while an engineering profile measures the cost of delivering visual experience to the learner. Finally, we study NorthCUA-Ultrafast to assess how direct action selection changes the balance between task success and execution latency.

sections.title: 6.2 GUI Grounding Results
sections.content: NorthCUA achieves state-of-the-art grounding results among the systems compared in Table 6, with Pro reaching 93.3% on SSP and 91.0% on OSWorld-G. The two benchmarks test complementary requirements, from locating small controls in dense professional interfaces to following functional and spatial instructions. We report the final long-horizon SFT checkpoints, using direct SSP inference and the Refined OSWorld-G instructions described in Section 6.1. Claude Opus 5.5 is the strongest reference on both benchmarks in this comparison, scoring 88.1% on SSP and 89.9% on OSWorld-G in our evaluation. Pro exceeds these scores by 5.2 and 1.1 percentage points, respectively. On SSP, Pro also leads Qwen3.8-Maxs reported 84.5% by 8.8 points. sections.title: 6.8 NorthCUA-Ultrafast
sections.content: Long computer-use tasks accumulate the latency of many successive model decisions. Some decisions require open-ended content, but others reduce to choosing an operation and control already present on the page. Predicting these finite choices directly could remove the decoding cost of routine actions. Jev provides relevant interface for this purpose by answering structured choice questions without generating their answers token by token (Almeida, 2026). We adapt this idea to NorthCUA-Nano through NorthCUA-Ultrafast, which combines choice head for finite decisions with the original models generation path for open-ended outputs. Figure 32 illustrates the resulting division of work. The classifier receives the task and recorded interaction history, including page observations, screenshots, and action overlays. Candidate controls are bound to the latest valid page observation for execution. One backbone forward pass supplies the features used to score the operation and its applicable targets. selected click, hover, or checkbox change can then be converted directly into tool call. The executor validates the returned tool and arguments, and uncertain finite choices can fall back to native generation. This preserves the original output interface while allowing routine finite actions to bypass decoding. Appendix E.7.4 specifies the routing and validation profiles. We study how much adaptation this choice interface requires, starting from the long-horizonSFT NorthCUA-Nano checkpoint before joint RL. sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: NorthCUA connects computer-use learning with the tasks and execution systems that supply its experience. We review these foundations in three parts. We first discuss policies and learning methods, then the construction of tasks and experience, and finally the harnesses and infrastructure that support their collection and use in training. NorthCUA Technical Report 74 / 123 NorthCUA 7 Related Work Computer-use policies and learning. Accurate GUI actions depend on linking instructions to screen elements. SeeClick studies grounding pre-training (Cheng et al., 2024). GUI-Actor develops attention-based pointing, while GUI-Cursor refines cursor movements through visual feedback (Wu et al., 2025, Zhao et al., 2026). End-to-end policies build on this capability to coordinate actions over time. UI-TARS integrates perception, reasoning, and action prediction, and OpenCUA develops reflective supervision from human demonstrations (Qin et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025c). Learning from outcomes offers further source of improvement. ComputerRL scales live-desktop RL (Lai et al., 2026), while VEM learns offline value estimates to guide environment-free policy exploration (Chen et al., 2026b). UI-TARS-2 and Qwen-CUA connect staged training with interactive learning (Wang et al., 2025a, Lu et al., 2026). For long trajectories, learning methods also specify how history and outcome feedback are carried across training segments. ScaleCUA masks reused history and shares rollout rewards and advantages across segments (Lv et al., 2026). Qwen-CUA preserves episode credit across slices and normalizes each trajectorys objective over active policy tokens (Lu et al., 2026). NorthCUA combines broad GUI mid-training, verified long-horizon SFT, and joint desktopweb RL. Our emphasis is on integrating decision-time input preservation and complete-attempt weighting with the Harness and experience-production pipeline. Scalable tasks and experience. Scaling workflow learning creates corresponding demand for executable tasks and reliable outcomes. OS-Genesis derives tasks from exploratory interaction (Sun et al., 2025), while GUI-360 combines sourced requests, environment templates, execution, and filtering for Windows data collection (Mu et al., 2025). ProCUA-SFT grounds tasks in real materials and checks preconditions before rollout (Jung et al., 2026). For outcome-driven learning, CUA-Gym and Qwen-UI-Agent synthesize compatible tasks, initial states, and verifiers (Wang et al., 2026a, Zhou et al., 2026b). WEFT extends this whole-system view to tooluse post-training, using execution feedback to revise interacting components and fresh rollouts to evaluate each revision (Mao et al., 2026). NorthCUA organizes construction around available software and content, sourced requests, or verified seed tasks. Each route produces an executable CaseSpec. separate grounding route uses application documentation to identify control functions and construct screenshotquerylocation supervision. Hard tasks also motivate retaining procedural knowledge across executions. Work2Skill turns synchronized human GUI demonstrations into reusable skills through on-demand inspection of action, visual, and available accessibility evidence (Huang et al., 2026). WebXSkill extracts executable procedures with language guidance from trajectories (Wang et al., 2026c). Search complements procedural guidance by considering alternative decisions. Computer-Using World Model simulates UI transitions for action selection (Guan et al., 2026), and Everything of Thoughts combines learned guidance with tree search for reasoning (Ding et al., 2024). Our RSI collection retains validated textual skills and real workspace checkpoints, so later attempts can reuse procedures or resume partial progress before full-task verification. Agent harnesses and learning infrastructure. Such collection and learning require an execution layer that preserves both software state and training evidence. UFO introduces hierarchical Windows interaction (Zhang et al., 2025c). UFO2 adds application-specialized agents and GUIAPI integration (Zhang et al., 2026), and UFO3 extends orchestration to heterogeneous devices through task DAG (Zhang et al., 2025d). For reuse across training systems, Agent Lightning v1.0 separates harness execution from RL optimization (He et al., 2026). Orchard provides shared sandbox lifecycle services (Peng et al., 2026), while Polar reconstructs tokenNorthCUA Technical Report 75 / 123 NorthCUA 8 Limitations and Responsible Use faithful training trajectories from recorded model calls (Xu et al., 2026a). NorthCUA focuses on integrating these system responsibilities for stateful visual interaction. Its shared desktop/web runtime, live outcome inspection, and parallel lifecycle service support experience collection. The Experience Adapter then preserves the recorded decisions when converting online attempts into learning samples, connecting execution and assessment to policy training through the same task and outcome interfaces.

sections.title: Limitations and Responsible Use
sections.content: Generalization and coverage. NorthCUA operates across diverse applications, while unfamiliar software and changing interface conventions remain challenging. Documentation-guided grounding expands the functional knowledge available during data construction, and skilland milestone-guided collection revisit workflows that ordinary attempts leave unfinished. Extending this coverage to new software and maintaining reliable execution as applications evolve remain important directions for the experience pipeline. Feedback and optimization. Executable verifiers and live-workspace inspection tie learning feedback to the work actually produced. Feedback quality depends on predicate coverage and the calibration of model judgments for open-ended content (Zheng et al., 2023). Controlled verifier probes and evidence-linked judgments help check both. Long workflows also concentrate many decisions into terminal outcome. More informative intermediate feedback could improve credit assignment and help agents reach correct results with fewer unnecessary actions. Responsible deployment. Isolated workspaces, explicit tool profiles, and retained execution records provide controls for deployment. Operating real software also requires authorized access, least-privilege credentials, and confirmation for consequential actions. External pages and documents can carry indirect prompt injections (Debenedetti et al., 2024), motivating adversarial testing appropriate to each application. Released materials should undergo licensing, privacy, and credential review alongside the operational checks.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented NorthCUA, an integrated system for developing computer-use agents through experience at scale. By connecting the NorthCUA Harness, Experience Flywheel, and Staged Learning through shared tasks and outcome checks, the system supports learning from both verified demonstrations and fresh policy interaction. Improved policies can return to the same infrastructure to collect further experience. Recursive self-improvement extends collection to diﬀicult workflows by preserving useful procedures and verified milestones, allowing later attempts to build on earlier progress. Across six benchmarks, the Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models in GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction. At 397B parameters, Pro outperforms the trillion-parameter general-purpose baselines on both grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified. Stage comparisons further show improvements in desktop and Web execution across all three model sizes following long-horizon NorthCUA Technical Report 76 / 123 NorthCUA References SFT and joint RL. Alongside these gains in task completion, NorthCUA-Ultrafast explores complementary route to faster decision-making. We release the three models, the full Harness code, and this technical report so that the work can be extended at both the policy and system levels. Together, they provide an open foundation for adapting agents to new software and developing better ways to collect and learn from experience. The broader goal is to make reliable software execution general AI capability, allowing users to delegate complete workflows from intent to verifiable outcome.

sections.content: The executable task, its workspace, and the resulting learning samples share an attempt identity. CaseSpec binds the request to its materials, initial state, and execution settings. The Experience Adapter retains the policys decision-time inputs when constructing samples, and the learner associates those samples with their attempt-level feedback. A.1 Information and Permission Boundaries Construction, execution, evaluation, and learning use different information. sections.content: This appendix defines the runtime choices needed to interpret an interaction record, including the observations presented to the policy, the tools available to each role, environment ownership, and demonstration selection. The learning-side segment and update rules are consolidated in Appendix E.5. H.1 Runtime Configuration context profile determines which retained interactions enter each model call. The sliding visual profile counts the latest clean frame within its image budget and keeps textual action/result records after image eviction. Other profiles replay visual history within compaction epoch. Text windows, image budgets, and semantic compaction are separate settings. The generic context manager defaults to off. Shadow mode records decisions without applying them, and enforce mode applies its configured policy. Historical overlays mark issued actions on pre-action images, while the latest clean frame shows the currently observed state. Text-only tools, including notes, do not add visual frames. later application change can require waiting or fresh observation. After timeout or failed refresh, state inspection precedes retry. Web element references belong to the observed page state, and failed refreshes invalidate affected aliases. Compaction retains structured account of the goal, constraints, supported facts, completed work, failures, current state, open items, and artifact references. Summaries and notes carry their temporal provenance and remain distinguishable from observations. The summary prompt, protected recent interactions, trigger/target budgets, and failure policy determine the resulting input. Note categories are fact, correction, precaution, constraint, decision, and checkpoint. Compatibility names map mistake to correction and plan/other to checkpoint. The exposed schema, replacement behavior, and prompt budget control which notes remain visible. Execution scopes and tool interfaces. session binds the agent to its environment and resources. round tracks one request and execution budget, and step records one policydecision and action-execution iteration. step can contain several tool calls, so model decisions, tool calls, and GUI interactions are different counts. The dispatcher validates declared arguments before invoking local handlers or connected MCP tools and returns results to the requesting step. Appendix H.2 specifies the model-facing interfaces. Runtime probes use separate permission profile from actor tools. Evaluator profiles and attribution. Evaluation binds task and rubric to an evidence source, inspection permissions, budget, and report schema. The rubric-generation template requests three to seven criteria. The Agent Kit desktop entry path can use request-level fallback, while the web profile supplies eight fixed criteria. The selected profile determines which criteria, weights, applicability rules, and reward conversion apply. Report-format validation checks the reports structure. Artifact tools inspect retained records. Live tools additionally require authorization and dispatcher bound to the evaluated workspace. Artifact-only replay has no live device access. Readonly probes are preferred. Shell inspection uses an allowlist, and state-changing GUI or browser NorthCUA Technical Report 105 / 123 NorthCUA Runtime and Admission Protocols inspection requires explicit permission. The workspace remains reserved through required live checks. Actor credit depends on the state before evaluator intervention. Terminal evidence and evaluator actions are therefore recorded separately.
